subject: The Arts

sources.title: NZC The Arts Years 0–10, September 2026
sources.status: published-final; Gazette pending; proposed Years 9–10 from 2027, Years 0–8 from 2029; transition applies

topics.name: Moving through space
topics.description: Dance can use movements at different levels, in different directions and along different pathways.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9–10, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: moving through space.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Travel along a curved route through the available space.
misconceptions: A dance pathway only describes a dancer's costume.
topics.question: How could a dancer show a curved pathway?
topics.answer: Travel along a curved route through the available space.
topics.explanation: Dance can use movements at different levels, in different directions and along different pathways.
hints: Think about the path the body travels.
Could the path bend rather than go straight?
topics.activity: Draw two pathways, then explore each slowly in a clear space.

topics.name: Moving to a beat
topics.description: Dancers can repeat and vary movements in time with a steady beat or a rhythmic pattern.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9–10, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: moving to a beat.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The movement's tempo becomes faster.
misconceptions: A faster movement always uses a larger space.
topics.question: What changes if a dancer repeats a step more quickly?
topics.answer: The movement's tempo becomes faster.
topics.explanation: Dancers can repeat and vary movements in time with a steady beat or a rhythmic pattern.
hints: Listen to how quickly the steps occur.
The word tempo describes speed.
topics.activity: Clap a steady pulse and explore one safe movement at two different speeds.

topics.name: Role and voice in drama
topics.description: In drama, a performer can use voice, gesture and movement to suggest a role or situation.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 > Drama; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: role and voice in drama.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: For example, they might use an energetic voice and expressive gesture appropriate to the role.
misconceptions: A dramatic role can only be communicated through costume.
topics.question: How could a performer show that a fictional character is excited?
topics.answer: For example, they might use an energetic voice and expressive gesture appropriate to the role.
topics.explanation: In drama, a performer can use voice, gesture and movement to suggest a role or situation.
hints: Think about voice as well as movement.
What might the character's body language show?
topics.activity: Act out two fictional moods using voice or gesture, and ask a partner what they notice.

topics.name: A still image in drama
topics.description: A still image made with bodies can represent a moment, relationship or idea in a dramatic scene.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 > Drama; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: a still image in drama.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They could freeze in poses that suggest waiting and looking for a bus.
misconceptions: A dramatic scene must always involve continuous speech.
topics.question: How might a group show that characters are waiting for a bus using a still image?
topics.answer: They could freeze in poses that suggest waiting and looking for a bus.
topics.explanation: A still image made with bodies can represent a moment, relationship or idea in a dramatic scene.
hints: Choose one clear moment.
How could posture and gaze help the audience?
topics.activity: Create a safe freeze-frame of a fictional scene and describe what the audience might infer.

topics.name: Pulse and rhythm
topics.description: A pulse is a steady beat; a rhythm is a pattern of longer and shorter sounds or silences.
topics.locator: PDF p. 12–13, Phase 1 > Music; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: pulse and rhythm.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Yes. Different sound patterns can occur while the underlying beat stays steady.
misconceptions: The rhythm and the steady beat are always identical.
topics.question: Can two different rhythms fit over the same steady beat?
topics.answer: Yes. Different sound patterns can occur while the underlying beat stays steady.
topics.explanation: A pulse is a steady beat; a rhythm is a pattern of longer and shorter sounds or silences.
hints: Tap a regular beat.
Can you clap two different patterns while keeping that beat?
topics.activity: Tap a steady pulse while a partner claps two different short patterns.

topics.name: Pitch and loudness
topics.description: Pitch describes how high or low a sound is; dynamics describe how loud or soft it is.
topics.locator: PDF p. 12–13, Phase 1 > Music; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: pitch and loudness.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Its loudness or dynamic changed.
misconceptions: A louder sound is automatically higher in pitch.
topics.question: If a note becomes louder without changing pitch, which musical quality changed?
topics.answer: Its loudness or dynamic changed.
topics.explanation: Pitch describes how high or low a sound is; dynamics describe how loud or soft it is.
hints: Did the note get higher or lower?
Think about loud and soft.
topics.activity: Hum or play one comfortable note softly and then more loudly, noticing that pitch need not change.

topics.name: Lines and shapes in art
topics.description: Artists can use different lines and shapes to organise an image and communicate an idea.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 1 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: lines and shapes in art.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It could suggest the flowing path or movement of the water.
misconceptions: Every line communicates exactly the same visual effect.
topics.question: How could a curved line contribute to a picture of moving water?
topics.answer: It could suggest the flowing path or movement of the water.
topics.explanation: Artists can use different lines and shapes to organise an image and communicate an idea.
hints: Think about how water might move.
Which kind of line could suggest a bend or wave?
topics.activity: Make two small drawings using straight and curved lines and describe the effect of each.

topics.name: Choosing colours for an artwork
topics.description: Artists select colours for many purposes, including drawing attention, creating contrast or expressing an idea.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 1 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: choosing colours for an artwork.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The difference in colour or brightness creates contrast.
misconceptions: A colour always has the same meaning for everyone.
topics.question: How might a bright shape stand out against a dark background?
topics.answer: The difference in colour or brightness creates contrast.
topics.explanation: Artists select colours for many purposes, including drawing attention, creating contrast or expressing an idea.
hints: Compare the shape with its surroundings.
Which difference makes the shape easier to notice?
topics.activity: Create two small images using the same shape on different backgrounds and compare their visibility.

topics.name: Sequencing dance movements
topics.description: A dance phrase combines movements in a chosen order and can be repeated or varied to communicate an idea.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 > Dance; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: sequencing dance movements.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The audience sees a different sequence and may interpret the relationship between movements differently.
misconceptions: The order of movements cannot affect a dance.
topics.question: Why might changing the order of two movements change a dance phrase?
topics.answer: The audience sees a different sequence and may interpret the relationship between movements differently.
topics.explanation: A dance phrase combines movements in a chosen order and can be repeated or varied to communicate an idea.
hints: What happens first in each version?
Does the second version lead the eye in the same way?
topics.activity: Create a short safe movement phrase, reverse its order and describe the difference.

topics.name: Energy and dynamics in dance
topics.description: Movement can vary in energy and quality, such as a sustained movement or a sudden one, to create different effects.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 > Dance; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: energy and dynamics in dance.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They could perform it quickly and sharply after a pause.
misconceptions: The same movement always communicates the same feeling.
topics.question: How could a dancer make a movement feel more sudden?
topics.answer: They could perform it quickly and sharply after a pause.
topics.explanation: Movement can vary in energy and quality, such as a sustained movement or a sudden one, to create different effects.
hints: Compare a slow continuous action with a quick one.
What effect might a pause have?
topics.activity: Explore a comfortable arm movement slowly and sharply, then describe each effect.

topics.name: Character and motivation
topics.description: A performer's choices can suggest what a character wants and how that influences the character's actions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 2 > Drama; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: character and motivation.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They could search the room and ask another character for help.
misconceptions: A character's actions never relate to what they want.
topics.question: A character wants to find a lost bag. What action could show that goal?
topics.answer: They could search the room and ask another character for help.
topics.explanation: A performer's choices can suggest what a character wants and how that influences the character's actions.
hints: What is the character trying to do?
Which action would help them do it?
topics.activity: Improvise a short fictional scene with a clear goal and discuss which actions showed it.

topics.name: Building dramatic tension
topics.description: A scene can create tension when an audience anticipates what might happen or how a problem will be resolved.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 2 > Drama; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: building dramatic tension.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It can build anticipation about what is inside.
misconceptions: Tension means a scene must contain real danger.
topics.question: How could a pause before opening a mysterious box affect an audience?
topics.answer: It can build anticipation about what is inside.
topics.explanation: A scene can create tension when an audience anticipates what might happen or how a problem will be resolved.
hints: What does the audience not yet know?
How might delaying the reveal affect them?
topics.activity: Create a short scene with a safe fictional surprise and try it with and without a pause.

topics.name: Repeating and varying musical patterns
topics.description: Musicians can repeat a pattern and change part of it to create a recognisable variation.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18–19, Phase 2 > Music; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: repeating and varying musical patterns.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Most of the pattern remained recognisable while its ending changed.
misconceptions: A variation must change every part of the original pattern.
topics.question: If a four-beat pattern is repeated with a different final sound, what stayed the same?
topics.answer: Most of the pattern remained recognisable while its ending changed.
topics.explanation: Musicians can repeat a pattern and change part of it to create a recognisable variation.
hints: Compare the first three beats.
What happened to the final sound?
topics.activity: Clap a four-beat pattern twice, changing one sound on the second repetition.

topics.name: Representing duration in music
topics.description: Notation and other agreed symbols can represent the relative duration of sounds and rests.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18–19, Phase 2 > Music; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: representing duration in music.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The longer sound lasts for two of the shorter durations.
misconceptions: Written symbols can never represent silence or duration.
topics.question: If one symbol lasts twice as long as another, how do their durations compare?
topics.answer: The longer sound lasts for two of the shorter durations.
topics.explanation: Notation and other agreed symbols can represent the relative duration of sounds and rests.
hints: Imagine two equal short beats.
Which symbol covers both beats?
topics.activity: Create a simple key for long and short sounds, write a pattern and perform it.

topics.name: Composition and visual focus
topics.description: Placement, size and contrast can direct attention within an artwork.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 2 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: composition and visual focus.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They might place it against a contrasting background or use a clear area around it.
misconceptions: The largest object must always be the focus of every artwork.
topics.question: How might an artist draw attention to a small object in a busy picture?
topics.answer: They might place it against a contrasting background or use a clear area around it.
topics.explanation: Placement, size and contrast can direct attention within an artwork.
hints: What surrounds the object?
Could contrast make it easier to notice?
topics.activity: Rearrange three paper shapes twice to create different focal points and explain your choices.

topics.name: Artworks and their contexts
topics.description: An artwork can be connected to the artist's intentions, community and cultural context. Interpretation benefits from reliable information and multiple viewpoints.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 2 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: artworks and their contexts.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Context can provide evidence about the artist's choices and the meanings they intended or communities understand.
misconceptions: A viewer can always know an artwork's cultural meaning from appearance alone.
topics.question: Why should a viewer learn about the context of an artwork?
topics.answer: Context can provide evidence about the artist's choices and the meanings they intended or communities understand.
topics.explanation: An artwork can be connected to the artist's intentions, community and cultural context. Interpretation benefits from reliable information and multiple viewpoints.
hints: Who made the work?
What information about its setting might help?
topics.activity: Look at an attributed public artwork and record an observation, a sourced context detail and one question.

topics.name: Unison and canon in dance
topics.description: Dancers can perform a movement at the same time or begin it at different times to create contrasting group structures.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 > Dance; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: unison and canon in dance.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: In unison dancers act together; in canon a movement is repeated by dancers at different times.
misconceptions: Canon and unison always have identical timing.
topics.question: What is the difference between unison and canon?
topics.answer: In unison dancers act together; in canon a movement is repeated by dancers at different times.
topics.explanation: Dancers can perform a movement at the same time or begin it at different times to create contrasting group structures.
hints: Do the dancers start together?
What happens when another dancer begins later?
topics.activity: Create a short safe phrase and perform it together, then as a staggered sequence.

topics.name: Choreographic choices and meaning
topics.description: A choreographer can select movement, timing and relationships between dancers to express an intention.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 > Dance; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: choreographic choices and meaning.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It can suggest a different relationship, such as closeness or separation, depending on context.
misconceptions: Changing spacing cannot affect an audience's interpretation.
topics.question: How might changing the distance between dancers affect a scene?
topics.answer: It can suggest a different relationship, such as closeness or separation, depending on context.
topics.explanation: A choreographer can select movement, timing and relationships between dancers to express an intention.
hints: Look at where the dancers are in relation to each other.
What could moving closer or farther apart suggest?
topics.activity: Make two versions of a short movement phrase with different spacing and explain the intended effect.

topics.name: Improvising a dramatic scene
topics.description: Improvisation develops a scene through responsive choices made in the moment, often with other performers.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 3 > Drama; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: improvising a dramatic scene.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Acknowledge the offer and respond in a way that develops the scene while respecting the shared situation.
misconceptions: Improvisation requires ignoring what other performers contribute.
topics.question: What could you do if a scene partner introduces a new fictional problem?
topics.answer: Acknowledge the offer and respond in a way that develops the scene while respecting the shared situation.
topics.explanation: Improvisation develops a scene through responsive choices made in the moment, often with other performers.
hints: Listen to the partner's idea.
What action could build on it?
topics.activity: Improvise a short scene around a fictional problem, then identify a choice that developed the story.

topics.name: Rehearsal and feedback
topics.description: Performers can rehearse, seek specific feedback and revise choices to make dramatic meaning clearer.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 3 > Drama; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: rehearsal and feedback.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Specific feedback about an observable choice and its effect is useful, such as whether the audience could understand the character's goal.
misconceptions: Feedback is useful only when it says whether a performance was good or bad.
topics.question: What kind of feedback would help a performer improve a scene?
topics.answer: Specific feedback about an observable choice and its effect is useful, such as whether the audience could understand the character's goal.
topics.explanation: Performers can rehearse, seek specific feedback and revise choices to make dramatic meaning clearer.
hints: Describe something you saw or heard.
Connect it to the scene's intended effect.
topics.activity: Rehearse a short scene and exchange one specific observation and one possible improvement.

topics.name: Musical texture and layers
topics.description: Musical texture describes how sound layers combine, for example a melody with an accompaniment.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24–25, Phase 3 > Music; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: musical texture and layers.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The texture gains another layer; its effect depends on how the parts interact.
misconceptions: Texture only describes how loud one sound is.
topics.question: What happens to texture when a second independent musical part is added?
topics.answer: The texture gains another layer; its effect depends on how the parts interact.
topics.explanation: Musical texture describes how sound layers combine, for example a melody with an accompaniment.
hints: How many parts were heard before?
How many are heard after the addition?
topics.activity: Create a short rhythm and add a second layer; describe how the combined sound changes.

topics.name: Music and cultural context
topics.description: Music can express ideas and connect people to communities and histories. Interpretations should be grounded in attributed sources and relevant community voices.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24–25, Phase 3 > Music; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: music and cultural context.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Context may explain its purpose, traditions or the choices of its creators and community.
misconceptions: All music from a community has a single identical meaning.
topics.question: Why might learning about a piece's context change how a listener understands it?
topics.answer: Context may explain its purpose, traditions or the choices of its creators and community.
topics.explanation: Music can express ideas and connect people to communities and histories. Interpretations should be grounded in attributed sources and relevant community voices.
hints: Who created or performs the music?
What purpose or setting might the source describe?
topics.activity: Listen to an appropriately attributed public example and identify one musical feature and one sourced context detail.

topics.name: Testing and refining visual ideas
topics.description: Artists can test materials, evaluate visual choices and revise a work in response to an intention or feedback.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 3 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: testing and refining visual ideas.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: They could increase contrast or adjust the label's size or placement.
misconceptions: An artwork cannot be changed once the first idea is drawn.
topics.question: If a drawn label is hard to read against its background, what could the artist change?
topics.answer: They could increase contrast or adjust the label's size or placement.
topics.explanation: Artists can test materials, evaluate visual choices and revise a work in response to an intention or feedback.
hints: Compare the label with its background.
What would make the letters easier to distinguish?
topics.activity: Make two small versions of a poster element, test readability and explain one revision.

topics.name: Interpreting visual evidence
topics.description: Viewers can support an interpretation of an artwork by pointing to specific visual features and considering context.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 3 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: interpreting visual evidence.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The repeated arrows are visible features that suggest direction; the viewer should also consider the poster's context.
misconceptions: An interpretation never needs evidence from the artwork.
topics.question: A poster uses repeated large arrows. What evidence supports an interpretation about movement or direction?
topics.answer: The repeated arrows are visible features that suggest direction; the viewer should also consider the poster's context.
topics.explanation: Viewers can support an interpretation of an artwork by pointing to specific visual features and considering context.
hints: Which visual feature repeats?
What does an arrow commonly indicate?
topics.activity: Choose an attributed image and support one interpretation with two observed features.

topics.name: Structuring choreography
topics.description: A choreographer can develop movement motifs and organise them into sections that support an artistic intention.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28–29, Phase 4 > Dance; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: structuring choreography.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It can make an idea recognisable and connect different sections, depending on how it is used.
misconceptions: A repeated movement can never contribute to meaning.
topics.question: How might repeating a movement motif affect a dance?
topics.answer: It can make an idea recognisable and connect different sections, depending on how it is used.
topics.explanation: A choreographer can develop movement motifs and organise them into sections that support an artistic intention.
hints: What does the audience see more than once?
How could repetition connect separate moments?
topics.activity: Plan a short sequence with a recurring movement and one deliberate variation; explain its purpose.

topics.name: Interpreting dance in context
topics.description: Interpretations of dance can draw on movement features, performance choices and cultural or historical context, with care for community-specific meaning.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28–29, Phase 4 > Dance; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: interpreting dance in context.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The meaning and appropriate interpretation may depend on the creators, community and context.
misconceptions: The same movement always has a single universal cultural meaning.
topics.question: Why should a viewer avoid assigning a universal meaning to a culturally specific dance?
topics.answer: The meaning and appropriate interpretation may depend on the creators, community and context.
topics.explanation: Interpretations of dance can draw on movement features, performance choices and cultural or historical context, with care for community-specific meaning.
hints: Whose knowledge should be consulted?
Can different performances have different purposes?
topics.activity: Use an attributed performance description to connect one movement choice with a sourced context detail.

topics.name: Structuring a dramatic scene
topics.description: A scene can organise action, tension and changes in relationships to shape how an audience understands a story.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30–31, Phase 4 > Drama; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: structuring a dramatic scene.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: A new event or choice can shift the conflict, a relationship or the direction of the action.
misconceptions: Every scene must present events without any change or development.
topics.question: How might a scene's turning point change the audience's understanding?
topics.answer: A new event or choice can shift the conflict, a relationship or the direction of the action.
topics.explanation: A scene can organise action, tension and changes in relationships to shape how an audience understands a story.
hints: What was happening before the change?
What becomes different afterwards?
topics.activity: Plan a fictional scene with an opening situation, a turning point and a response.

topics.name: Analysing performance choices
topics.description: Performers and directors use choices such as space, voice, movement and timing to shape an audience's response.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30–31, Phase 4 > Drama; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: analysing performance choices.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: It might suggest distance or conflict, depending on the surrounding action and context.
misconceptions: Staging choices cannot influence meaning.
topics.question: How could moving two characters apart change a scene?
topics.answer: It might suggest distance or conflict, depending on the surrounding action and context.
topics.explanation: Performers and directors use choices such as space, voice, movement and timing to shape an audience's response.
hints: Consider the characters' positions.
What relationship could the new spacing suggest?
topics.activity: Rehearse the same short scene with two different spatial arrangements and compare the effects.

topics.name: Arranging musical parts
topics.description: An arrangement selects and organises musical parts for performers or instruments, taking balance, texture and purpose into account.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32–34, Phase 4 > Music; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: arranging musical parts.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: A different instrument can change timbre, balance or the way the melody stands out.
misconceptions: Changing an instrument can never affect a piece's sound.
topics.question: Why might an arranger change which instrument plays a melody?
topics.answer: A different instrument can change timbre, balance or the way the melody stands out.
topics.explanation: An arrangement selects and organises musical parts for performers or instruments, taking balance, texture and purpose into account.
hints: Think about the sound quality of each instrument.
Which choice best suits the intended effect?
topics.activity: Plan two arrangements of a short melody with different sound sources and explain the intended contrast.

topics.name: Using music technology purposefully
topics.description: Digital music tools can record, arrange or modify sound. Choices about effects and levels should serve the intended musical result.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32–34, Phase 4 > Music; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: using music technology purposefully.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The effect may obscure an important part or conflict with the intended sound.
misconceptions: Adding more effects always improves a recording.
topics.question: Why might a musician reduce an effect after listening to a recording?
topics.answer: The effect may obscure an important part or conflict with the intended sound.
topics.explanation: Digital music tools can record, arrange or modify sound. Choices about effects and levels should serve the intended musical result.
hints: Can the listener hear the main part clearly?
What happens when the effect is reduced?
topics.activity: If suitable equipment is available, compare a short sound with and without an effect; otherwise discuss a supplied example.

topics.name: Visual choices and artistic intention
topics.description: Artists develop ideas using media, techniques and composition, and evaluate how well those choices communicate an intention.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Phase 4 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: visual choices and artistic intention.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: Use clear contrast, a legible type size and a focused layout.
misconceptions: Visual choices do not affect how an audience accesses a message.
topics.question: An artist wants a poster to be readable from a distance. What choice could help?
topics.answer: Use clear contrast, a legible type size and a focused layout.
topics.explanation: Artists develop ideas using media, techniques and composition, and evaluate how well those choices communicate an intention.
hints: How far away is the viewer?
Which visual choices make text easier to read?
topics.activity: Create a small poster draft, test it at a distance and revise one feature based on the result.

topics.name: Art, attribution and cultural context
topics.description: Visual art can draw on particular cultural knowledge and traditions. Respectful study identifies creators and sources and avoids treating culturally specific forms as free templates.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Phase 4 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level editorial alignment
objectives: Explain or demonstrate: art, attribution and cultural context.
evidence: Answers the example question with a relevant explanation: The form may have a particular creator, community meaning or conditions for appropriate use.
misconceptions: All culturally significant designs can be copied without context or permission.
topics.question: Why should a student seek reliable attribution and guidance before using a culturally specific design?
topics.answer: The form may have a particular creator, community meaning or conditions for appropriate use.
topics.explanation: Visual art can draw on particular cultural knowledge and traditions. Respectful study identifies creators and sources and avoids treating culturally specific forms as free templates.
hints: Who created or holds knowledge of the work?
Does the source explain whether adaptation is appropriate?
topics.activity: Study an attributed public artwork and write a response about its visible features and documented context without copying a protected design.

topics.name: Mirroring a movement
topics.description: Dancers can respond to each other by copying a movement as if looking into a mirror. Clear, slow movements and enough space help partners see and follow one another.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9–10, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate mirroring a movement using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Lift the opposite arm from their own point of view so that the shapes appear reflected.
misconceptions: Mirroring means both people must always move in the same direction across the room.
topics.question: One dancer lifts an arm slowly while facing a partner. What could the partner do to mirror them?
topics.answer: Lift the opposite arm from their own point of view so that the shapes appear reflected.
topics.explanation: In a mirror image the shapes face each other, so the partner responds across the shared space.
hints: Imagine looking at a reflection.
Which arm makes the two shapes appear symmetrical?
topics.activity: With a partner, try three slow mirrored arm shapes with room to move; a seated or imaginary partner version also works.

topics.name: Repeating and changing movement
topics.description: A repeated movement can establish a pattern. A contrasting movement, such as a change in size or speed, can make a difference visible to an audience.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9–10, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate repeating and changing movement using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The crouch contrasts with the two upward reaches.
misconceptions: Every movement in a dance must be different to make a pattern.
topics.question: A dancer reaches up twice and then crouches. Which part provides a contrast?
topics.answer: The crouch contrasts with the two upward reaches.
topics.explanation: The levels and actions change after the repeated reaching movement.
hints: Which movement happens twice?
What changes when the dancer crouches?
topics.activity: In a clear space, choose one comfortable movement, repeat it twice, add a different movement and describe the contrast.

topics.name: Actor and role
topics.description: An actor can represent an imagined character without being that character in everyday life. Voice, facial expression, gesture and posture can suggest the role to an audience.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate actor and role using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The explorer is an imagined role that the student is portraying.
misconceptions: An actor has to share a character's real experiences to play a role.
topics.question: A student pretends to be a nervous explorer in a story. Who is the explorer?
topics.answer: The explorer is an imagined role that the student is portraying.
topics.explanation: A role is created for the drama; it is separate from the performer outside the scene.
hints: Is the explorer a real identity the student must have?
What character is the student pretending to be?
topics.activity: Choose a fictional explorer and show curiosity through a gesture; observers describe what they noticed without judging the performer.

topics.name: Showing a setting
topics.description: A drama can suggest where a story takes place through words, actions, sound and a few chosen objects. A setting can be imagined even when the performance space remains unchanged.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate showing a setting using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They might mime holding a hat and use spoken words or gentle sound to suggest the wind.
misconceptions: A drama needs a full set of realistic scenery before a place can be imagined.
topics.question: In an empty classroom scene, how could actors suggest they are in a windy park?
topics.answer: They might mime holding a hat and use spoken words or gentle sound to suggest the wind.
topics.explanation: Coordinated performance choices give the audience clues about the imagined place.
hints: What could people do in wind?
Which sound or spoken clue could help the audience?
topics.activity: In a small group, create a safe ten-second scene in an imaginary place using a gesture and one sound; classmates name their evidence.

topics.name: Visual and tactile texture
topics.description: Texture can describe how a surface feels, such as smooth or rough, and how a surface looks as if it might feel. Artists can suggest texture with different marks and materials.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 1 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate visual and tactile texture using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: No. The marks suggest a visual texture; the paper may still feel smooth.
misconceptions: A picture of a rough surface must itself be rough to touch.
topics.question: A drawing uses many short marks to suggest rough bark. Is the roughness necessarily real to touch?
topics.answer: No. The marks suggest a visual texture; the paper may still feel smooth.
topics.explanation: Visual appearance and the actual tactile surface can differ.
hints: Is the bark in this example a drawing or a real surface?
What would a finger actually touch?
topics.activity: Make two small patches with dots, lines or crayon rubbing on safe surfaces, then describe the texture each suggests.

topics.name: Mixing colours
topics.description: Artists can mix primary paint colours to create secondary colours. Red and yellow paint, for example, can make orange, with the result varying according to the materials and proportions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 1 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate mixing colours using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Orange.
misconceptions: Every mixture gives exactly the same shade regardless of material and proportion.
topics.question: What secondary colour can red and yellow paint make together?
topics.answer: Orange.
topics.explanation: The mixture combines two primary colours; the proportions and particular paints affect its appearance.
hints: Think of a colour between red and yellow.
What colour might a citrus fruit of that name be?
topics.activity: With small amounts of paint or coloured pencils, explore red and yellow together, then compare two proportions and name the visible change.
materials: red and yellow paint or coloured pencils

topics.name: Dance formations and spacing
topics.description: A formation is how dancers are arranged in the performance space, such as a line or circle. The arrangement can change while performers keep a safe distance and respond to each other.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate dance formations and spacing using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The group's formation has changed.
misconceptions: Formation refers only to the speed of a dance.
topics.question: A group changes from a line to a circle. What has changed?
topics.answer: The group's formation has changed.
topics.explanation: The formation describes the relative arrangement of the dancers in space.
hints: Look at the shape the group makes together.
Did the dancers' arrangement stay in a line?
topics.activity: Sketch a line and a circle, then plan how a group could move safely between them; use counters if movement is unsuitable.

topics.name: Movement motif and variation
topics.description: A short movement idea can recur as a motif. Dancers can vary its direction, level, timing or energy while retaining a recognisable feature.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate movement motif and variation using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The level of the recurring reaching movement changes.
misconceptions: A variation must remove every connection with the original movement.
topics.question: A dancer repeats a reach but changes its level from high to low. What is the variation?
topics.answer: The level of the recurring reaching movement changes.
topics.explanation: The reaching action links the two versions, while the level provides a noticeable variation.
hints: What action is recognisable in both versions?
Which aspect of the movement changes?
topics.activity: Choose a comfortable two-action motif and sketch or perform a high and a low version, explaining what stayed recognisable.

topics.name: Dialogue and stage directions
topics.description: Dialogue is the words characters say. Stage directions give information about actions, movement, setting or delivery and are interpreted by performers.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 2 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate dialogue and stage directions using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: “She moves behind the chair” is the stage direction.
misconceptions: Every word printed in a script is spoken aloud by a character.
topics.question: A script says “Mara: Wait! (She moves behind the chair.)” Which part is the stage direction?
topics.answer: “She moves behind the chair” is the stage direction.
topics.explanation: That phrase describes an action; the word “Wait!” is spoken dialogue.
hints: Which part is said aloud by the character?
Which part tells a performer what to do?
topics.activity: Write two lines for fictional characters and add one bracketed action; read the dialogue and demonstrate the action in a safe space.

topics.name: How instruments produce sound
topics.description: Instruments can be grouped by how sound is produced, such as vibrating strings, air or struck surfaces. Instruments in a family can still sound distinct because their materials and shapes vary.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18–19, Phase 2 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate how instruments produce sound using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The string vibrates, and the instrument's body helps the sound be heard.
misconceptions: Instruments in the same broad family must sound identical.
topics.question: What produces the sound when a violin string is bowed?
topics.answer: The string vibrates, and the instrument's body helps the sound be heard.
topics.explanation: A bowed string moves back and forth; the vibrating body transfers sound to the surrounding air.
hints: Which part does the bow touch?
What does that part do when it makes a sound?
topics.activity: Look at pictures of a violin, drum and flute; match each to a vibrating string, struck surface or vibrating air, then discuss the evidence.
materials: pictures of a violin, drum and flute

topics.name: Musical phrases and structure
topics.description: A phrase is a recognisable musical idea that can repeat, change or answer another phrase. Larger structures organise sections, such as a recurring chorus and contrasting verse.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18–19, Phase 2 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate musical phrases and structure using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The chorus repeats.
misconceptions: A song needs a completely new idea in every section.
topics.question: A song returns to the same chorus after two different verses. Which section repeats?
topics.answer: The chorus repeats.
topics.explanation: The verse changes between statements while the chorus returns, helping organise the song.
hints: Which part comes back after each verse?
Is the returning section the verse or chorus?
topics.activity: Invent a four-beat phrase A and a different phrase B, then tap an A–B–A structure and explain which idea returns.

topics.name: Foreground, background and overlap
topics.description: Artists can suggest depth on a flat surface by overlapping shapes and placing forms in a foreground or background. An overlapping shape generally appears in front of the shape it partly covers.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 2 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate foreground, background and overlap using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The tree appears in front of the house.
misconceptions: An overlapping shape always appears behind the shape it covers.
topics.question: A tree is drawn over part of a house. Which appears closer to the viewer?
topics.answer: The tree appears in front of the house.
topics.explanation: The house is partly hidden by the tree, which gives a visual clue about their relative positions.
hints: Which object covers part of the other?
Does the covered object appear in front or behind?
topics.activity: Cut or draw three simple shapes, arrange one partly over another and label an imagined foreground and background.

topics.name: Light and dark tone
topics.description: Tone describes how light or dark a colour or mark appears. Artists can use a range of tones to suggest form, focus or mood.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 2 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate light and dark tone using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: It can suggest that light falls on one side and that the ball has form.
misconceptions: A drawing can only show form through its outline.
topics.question: A drawing has a light side and a dark side on a ball. What might the contrast suggest?
topics.answer: It can suggest that light falls on one side and that the ball has form.
topics.explanation: The tonal difference gives a visual clue about light and the rounded surface.
hints: Which side looks closer to a light source?
How do light and dark marks differ?
topics.activity: Shade a drawn circle from light to dark using a pencil or digital tool, then point to one mark that suggests a change in light.

topics.name: Relationships between dancers
topics.description: Choreographers can organise relationships between dancers through facing, proximity, mirroring, following and shared timing. Each choice changes how a viewer may interpret a group.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate relationships between dancers using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They change their spatial relationship by approaching and separating while facing each other.
misconceptions: A relationship in dance can only be shown by holding hands.
topics.question: Two dancers face each other and move closer, then move apart. What relationship can be observed?
topics.answer: They change their spatial relationship by approaching and separating while facing each other.
topics.explanation: The direction they face and the distance between them are visible features of their relationship.
hints: Where are they facing?
What happens to the distance between them?
topics.activity: Use two counters on paper to plan an approach and retreat; describe facing and distance, or perform it slowly in a clear space.

topics.name: Transitions between dance phrases
topics.description: A transition connects one movement phrase to another. Dancers can plan direction, energy and timing so the change contributes to the intended effect and remains safe.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate transitions between dance phrases using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A controlled movement that safely connects the low ending to the standing start.
misconceptions: The movements between phrases never affect a dance's meaning or flow.
topics.question: A dancer finishes low to the ground and begins the next phrase standing. What should they plan?
topics.answer: A controlled movement that safely connects the low ending to the standing start.
topics.explanation: The transition bridges different positions and affects how the audience experiences the sequence.
hints: Where does the first phrase end?
What movement connects that position to the next one?
topics.activity: Draw two starting and ending positions and invent a comfortable transition, offering a seated or imagined alternative where needed.

topics.name: Directing audience focus
topics.description: Performers can guide audience attention through position, movement, voice and contrast. Staging choices can make a character or action more noticeable without explaining everything in words.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 3 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate directing audience focus using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The moving character is likely to attract attention because the others remain still.
misconceptions: The audience always notices every part of a scene equally.
topics.question: In a still group scene, one character begins to move. Where might the audience focus?
topics.answer: The moving character is likely to attract attention because the others remain still.
topics.explanation: Movement contrasts with stillness, making that action more prominent.
hints: What is different about one character?
How does motion stand out against stillness?
topics.activity: Create a fictional three-person tableau and change one performer's movement; observers describe where they looked and why.

topics.name: Design choices and dramatic mood
topics.description: Lighting, sound, props and costume can support the mood and meaning of a scene. Their effect depends on the story, the audience and the choices made by the performers.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 3 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate design choices and dramatic mood using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The recurring sound could build an uneasy or curious mood, depending on how it is used.
misconceptions: A prop or sound always has one fixed meaning in every scene.
topics.question: A scene about a mysterious discovery uses a quiet repeated sound. How might that support the scene?
topics.answer: The recurring sound could build an uneasy or curious mood, depending on how it is used.
topics.explanation: A carefully chosen sound gives the audience a clue and can make anticipation grow.
hints: What might repetition make the audience expect?
How could a quiet sound affect the scene's mood?
topics.activity: Plan two safe sound choices for a short fictional scene and explain how each might affect audience interpretation; no equipment is required.

topics.name: Notes on a musical staff
topics.description: A staff uses five lines and four spaces to organise written pitches. The clef tells a reader which pitches those positions represent; a note's vertical position helps show its relative pitch.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24–25, Phase 3 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate notes on a musical staff using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: It indicates a higher written pitch.
misconceptions: A higher written note always means a louder note.
topics.question: On the same staff and clef, one note is written above another. What does its higher position generally indicate?
topics.answer: It indicates a higher written pitch.
topics.explanation: Within a given clef, notes placed higher on the staff represent higher pitches.
hints: Compare the notes' vertical positions.
What musical property does vertical position represent?
topics.activity: Draw a five-line staff and place two notes at different heights, then label which is higher without needing to name their exact pitches.

topics.name: Melody and accompaniment
topics.description: A melody is a sequence of pitches heard as a musical idea. Accompaniment supports it through other sounds, which may include chords, a bass line or a rhythmic pattern.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24–25, Phase 3 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate melody and accompaniment using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The singer's tune is the melody in this example.
misconceptions: Every sound in a piece has the same musical role.
topics.question: A singer performs a tune while a guitar plays supporting chords. Which part is the melody?
topics.answer: The singer's tune is the melody in this example.
topics.explanation: The tune is the principal pitched idea, and the guitar chords support it.
hints: Which part could be sung by itself as the tune?
Which part supplies supporting chords?
topics.activity: Tap a steady pattern while another person hums a short comfortable tune, or use written patterns; identify the melody and support.

topics.name: Choosing a visual medium
topics.description: A medium and its techniques affect what an artist can make visible. Drawing, collage, photography and other approaches offer different possibilities, and the choice should support the intended result.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 3 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate choosing a visual medium using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Collage could combine the cut shapes and text on one surface.
misconceptions: Every medium produces the same result regardless of materials or technique.
topics.question: An artist wants to combine cut-paper shapes with printed text. Which medium could support the idea?
topics.answer: Collage could combine the cut shapes and text on one surface.
topics.explanation: Collage allows different pieces of material to be selected, arranged and attached together.
hints: What materials does the artist want to combine?
Which approach assembles separate pieces?
topics.activity: Plan a small collage from scrap paper or a digital equivalent, arranging pieces before attaching them and explaining one material choice.

topics.name: Building tension across a scene
topics.description: Dramatic tension can develop as a character pursues an objective while facing an obstacle. Changes in pace, silence, information and interaction can shape how an audience anticipates the outcome.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30–31, Phase 4 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate building tension across a scene using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The time pressure and obstacle make the audience uncertain whether the character will find the key.
misconceptions: A scene has tension only if its performers shout.
topics.question: A character is searching for a key as the lights are about to go out. What creates tension?
topics.answer: The time pressure and obstacle make the audience uncertain whether the character will find the key.
topics.explanation: A clear goal, an obstacle and limited time create anticipation about what happens next.
hints: What does the character want?
What makes achieving the goal uncertain?
topics.activity: Write a short fictional scene outline with a goal, an obstacle and one change in pace, then explain its likely effect on an audience.

topics.name: Justifying production choices
topics.description: A production choice can be evaluated by connecting it to dramatic intention and observable audience effects. Designers and performers may revise voice, movement, sound, lighting or costume as the scene develops.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30–31, Phase 4 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate justifying production choices using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The pause can make the audience anticipate the answer and reveal the character's hesitation.
misconceptions: Any production choice is effective solely because it uses more equipment.
topics.question: A group chooses a long pause before a character answers. How could they justify it?
topics.answer: The pause can make the audience anticipate the answer and reveal the character's hesitation.
topics.explanation: The choice is linked to a specific point in the scene and a plausible effect on the audience.
hints: Where in the scene does the pause occur?
What might the audience expect during the pause?
topics.activity: Take a short fictional exchange, propose two different pauses or sound cues and explain the intended effect of each.

topics.name: The major scale pattern
topics.description: A major scale follows a sequence of tones and semitones. In C major the ascending notes C, D, E, F, G, A, B and C use no sharps or flats in the key signature.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32–33, Phase 4 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate the major scale pattern using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Between E and F, and between B and C.
misconceptions: Every step between neighbouring notes in a major scale is a whole tone.
topics.question: Between which adjacent notes in an ascending C major scale are the semitone steps?
topics.answer: Between E and F, and between B and C.
topics.explanation: Those two intervals complete the major-scale pattern of tones and semitones in C major.
hints: Write the notes from C up to the next C.
Which two pairs of adjacent letter names are a semitone apart on a keyboard?
topics.activity: Draw or inspect a keyboard diagram, label the C major notes and mark the two adjacent pairs with no black key between them.

topics.name: Building a tonic triad
topics.description: A tonic triad is built on the first note of a scale by combining the first, third and fifth scale degrees. In C major, the notes C, E and G form the tonic triad.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32–33, Phase 4 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate building a tonic triad using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: C, E and G.
misconceptions: A triad must use three consecutive notes of a scale.
topics.question: Which three notes form the tonic triad in C major?
topics.answer: C, E and G.
topics.explanation: They are the first, third and fifth notes of the C major scale.
hints: Write the C major scale in order.
Select scale degrees one, three and five.
topics.activity: Write the C major scale and circle its first, third and fifth notes; play or sing them only if a suitable instrument or comfortable voice is available.

topics.name: Framing and the rule of thirds
topics.description: The rule of thirds is one optional way to arrange a composition using a grid of three rows and columns. Placing a focal point near a grid intersection can change visual balance and emphasis; artists can also choose other arrangements.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Phase 4 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate framing and the rule of thirds using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They are exploring the rule of thirds.
misconceptions: The rule of thirds is compulsory for every successful image.
topics.question: A photographer places a subject near a grid intersection rather than in the centre. What compositional idea are they exploring?
topics.answer: They are exploring the rule of thirds.
topics.explanation: The subject has been placed using intersections in a three-by-three grid to consider balance and emphasis.
hints: Imagine dividing the frame into three equal rows and columns.
Where do those lines cross?
topics.activity: Sketch a simple scene twice, placing the same subject centrally and near a third-line intersection, then compare the emphasis; no real people need be photographed.

topics.name: Stillness in a dance
topics.description: A dancer can pause or hold a shape as part of a sequence. Stillness can create a clear beginning, ending or contrast with movement.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9–10, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate stillness in a dance using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The moving action becomes stillness or a held shape.
misconceptions: A dance must contain continuous movement with no pauses.
topics.question: A dancer moves across the space, then holds a shape. What changes when the dancer stops?
topics.answer: The moving action becomes stillness or a held shape.
topics.explanation: A deliberate pause changes the action and can make the preceding movement stand out.
hints: Does the body keep travelling?
What word describes a held position?
topics.activity: Create a three-part sequence with a comfortable starting shape, one movement and a still ending; adapt it for seated movement if needed.

topics.name: Gesture and expression
topics.description: A gesture is a meaningful movement of part of the body. In drama, performers can combine gesture, facial expression and voice to suggest how an imagined character feels or what they want.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate gesture and expression using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Pointing towards the door is the gesture.
misconceptions: Every gesture has a single fixed meaning in all places and cultures.
topics.question: An actor points towards a pretend door and steps back. What gesture gives the audience a clue?
topics.answer: Pointing towards the door is the gesture.
topics.explanation: The deliberate hand movement directs attention and contributes to the character's action.
hints: Which movement uses a hand?
Where does that movement draw attention?
topics.activity: Choose an imaginary object and show an action with one clear gesture; an observer describes the movement and one possible meaning.

topics.name: Sound and silence
topics.description: Music can organise both sounds and periods of silence. A pause can separate musical ideas or become part of a repeated rhythm.
topics.locator: PDF p. 12–13, Phase 1 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate sound and silence using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Yes. The silence occupies a place between the sounds.
misconceptions: Silence cannot be part of a musical pattern.
topics.question: A pattern goes tap, tap, silence, tap. Is the silence part of the pattern?
topics.answer: Yes. The silence occupies a place between the sounds.
topics.explanation: The pause is an intentional part of the order, so it helps define how the pattern is heard.
hints: What happens between the second and final tap?
Would the pattern sound the same if a tap replaced the pause?
topics.activity: Tap a four-beat pattern with one silent beat, then swap the silent beat and compare the two patterns; use visual marks as an alternative.

topics.name: Images can tell stories
topics.description: Artists can arrange people, objects, places and actions to suggest a story. Viewers can use details in the artwork as evidence while recognising that different interpretations are possible.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 1 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate images can tell stories using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The viewer might infer that it has recently rained, using the umbrella and puddle as clues.
misconceptions: An artwork can communicate a story only if every word is written on it.
topics.question: An illustration shows a person carrying an umbrella beside a puddle. What might a viewer infer?
topics.answer: The viewer might infer that it has recently rained, using the umbrella and puddle as clues.
topics.explanation: The objects provide evidence for a possible story, although the artist may have intended something different.
hints: Which objects are visible?
What weather might connect an umbrella with a puddle?
topics.activity: Draw an imaginary scene with two visual clues, then invite an observer to describe one possible story and identify the clues.

topics.name: Recognising timbre
topics.description: Timbre, or tone colour, is the quality that helps listeners distinguish sounds even when they have the same pitch and loudness. The way a sound is produced and the instrument's material can influence it.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18–19, Phase 2 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate recognising timbre using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Their timbre, or tone colour.
misconceptions: Two instruments playing the same pitch must have identical sounds.
topics.question: A flute and violin play the same note at a similar loudness but sound different. What quality helps distinguish them?
topics.answer: Their timbre, or tone colour.
topics.explanation: Different sound-producing materials and methods produce different sound qualities even at the same pitch.
hints: The note and loudness are similar. What else can sound different?
What term describes the character or quality of a sound?
topics.activity: Listen to two accessible credited instrument samples or imagine their sounds from descriptions, then list words that distinguish their qualities without ranking them.
materials: credited instrument samples or written descriptions

topics.name: Positive and negative space
topics.description: Positive space is occupied by a subject or form; negative space is the area around and between subjects. Both contribute to the composition and how easily the viewer recognises shapes.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 2 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate positive and negative space using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The sky area around the tree is negative space.
misconceptions: The area around a subject has no role in an artwork's composition.
topics.question: In a drawing of a tree against a plain sky, what is an example of negative space?
topics.answer: The sky area around the tree is negative space.
topics.explanation: The tree is the subject, while the surrounding area helps define its outline.
hints: Which shape is the main subject?
What area surrounds that subject?
topics.activity: Draw a simple object and colour only the space around it; compare how the empty shape helps define the object.

topics.name: Character viewpoint
topics.description: Characters may interpret the same event differently because of their goals, knowledge and relationships. Dramatic techniques can reveal these viewpoints through dialogue, movement or a character's private thoughts.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Phase 3 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate character viewpoint using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They may have different goals or knowledge about the situation.
misconceptions: Every character must interpret a shared event in the same way.
topics.question: Two characters both hear a locked door close. One is relieved and the other is worried. Why might they respond differently?
topics.answer: They may have different goals or knowledge about the situation.
topics.explanation: A shared event can have different significance for different characters, depending on what each wants or knows.
hints: Do the characters know or want exactly the same things?
What different goal could explain each response?
topics.activity: Write two fictional character statements about the same event, each with a different goal; identify the clue to each viewpoint.

topics.name: Rests in written music
topics.description: A rest is a written symbol for a measured period of silence. Its duration matters because the timing of the surrounding notes depends on how long the pause lasts.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24–25, Phase 3 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate rests in written music using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Four beats, including the silent beat.
misconceptions: A written rest has no duration because it makes no sound.
topics.question: A four-beat bar contains three one-beat notes and a one-beat rest. How many beats does the bar contain?
topics.answer: Four beats, including the silent beat.
topics.explanation: The three sounding beats and one silent beat together fill the four-beat bar.
hints: Count the three notes first.
Does a rest take time even though no sound is played?
topics.activity: Write or tap three beats followed by one silent beat in a four-count cycle; mark the pause visually if sound is unsuitable.

topics.name: Observation and proportion
topics.description: Observational drawing involves looking closely at a subject and considering the relative sizes and positions of its parts. An artist can revise marks as they compare their drawing with what they see.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 3 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate observation and proportion using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Look at the subject again, compare the handle with the cup and revise its size.
misconceptions: Observational drawing requires copying every detail immediately without revision.
topics.question: A cup handle appears too large compared with the cup. What could the artist do?
topics.answer: Look at the subject again, compare the handle with the cup and revise its size.
topics.explanation: Proportion describes a relationship between parts, so comparison helps the drawing better reflect the observation.
hints: What two parts are being compared?
Is the handle larger or smaller relative to the cup in the drawing?
topics.activity: Choose a simple object, sketch its outline and compare the size of two parts; revise one mark and note what changed.

topics.name: Refining dance through feedback
topics.description: Specific feedback about timing, spacing or movement quality can help a dancer revise a performance. The dancer can compare the feedback with their intention and decide what adjustment to try.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28–29, Phase 4 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate refining dance through feedback using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Increase or clarify the delay between entries and see whether the canon is easier to notice.
misconceptions: Useful feedback only says whether a performance was good or bad.
topics.question: A group receives feedback that its canon entries are hard to distinguish. What could they test?
topics.answer: Increase or clarify the delay between entries and see whether the canon is easier to notice.
topics.explanation: A more distinct interval can make the staggered timing visible while keeping the intended device.
hints: What makes a canon different from unison?
Which part of the timing might need to be clearer?
topics.activity: Plan a short canon with counters, ask an observer when each entry happens, and revise the spacing in time based on that evidence.

topics.name: Dramatic convention and effect
topics.description: A dramatic convention is an agreed way of presenting action, such as direct address to the audience or narration. A convention can shape what an audience knows and how it experiences a scene.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30–31, Phase 4 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate dramatic convention and effect using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Direct address to the audience.
misconceptions: Characters in drama can only speak to other characters on stage.
topics.question: A character pauses the scene to speak directly to the audience about a secret. What convention are they using?
topics.answer: Direct address to the audience.
topics.explanation: The performer communicates with the audience rather than only with other characters in the scene.
hints: Who is the character speaking to?
Are the other characters the intended listeners?
topics.activity: Write two lines for a fictional scene and add a short direct address; explain what the audience learns from it.

topics.name: Audio and MIDI in music production
topics.description: In a digital audio workstation, recorded audio stores a sound waveform, while MIDI stores performance information such as notes, timing and velocity. MIDI needs a sound-generating instrument or software to be heard.
topics.locator: PDF p. 34, Phase 4 > Music > Music Technology (optional); broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate audio and midi in music production using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A MIDI track, using a suitable software or connected instrument.
misconceptions: MIDI and recorded audio store exactly the same kind of information.
topics.question: A producer wants to change one entered note without re-recording a performance. Which type of track commonly allows direct note editing?
topics.answer: A MIDI track, using a suitable software or connected instrument.
topics.explanation: MIDI represents performance events that can be edited, whereas recorded audio is a captured sound waveform.
hints: Which track stores note events?
Which one stores a recorded waveform?
topics.activity: Sketch a fictional timeline with one audio track and one MIDI track, and label an edit appropriate to each; software use is optional.

topics.name: Colour contrast and intention
topics.description: Colour contrast can draw attention or create a particular relationship between parts of an image. Complementary colours sit opposite each other on a conventional colour wheel, and their effect depends on surrounding colours and proportions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Phase 4 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate colour contrast and intention using a relevant example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A complementary colour contrast.
misconceptions: A complementary colour pair always has exactly the same visual effect in every composition.
topics.question: An artist places blue beside orange to make a small shape stand out. What kind of colour relationship are they using?
topics.answer: A complementary colour contrast.
topics.explanation: Blue and orange are opposite on the conventional colour wheel, which can make their difference prominent.
hints: Find blue on a colour wheel.
Which colour is opposite blue?
topics.activity: Use a simple colour wheel to choose two complementary colours, arrange them in two proportions and compare which area attracts attention.

topics.name: Travelling and stationary dance movement
topics.description: A travelling movement carries the body from one place to another, while a stationary movement can change body shape without travelling. Dancers can combine both in a phrase.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Exploring and Creating, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate travelling and stationary dance movement in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The steps across the room travel; the bend happens in place.
misconceptions: Every movement that changes the shape of the body also travels to a new place.
topics.question: A dancer steps across a room and then bends in place. Which movement travels?
topics.answer: The steps across the room travel; the bend happens in place.
topics.explanation: The steps change location, whereas the bend changes shape without moving the whole body to a new place.
hints: Which action takes the dancer to a different place?
Does the bend need the dancer to travel across the room?
topics.activity: In a clear space, choose a comfortable travelling action and a stationary action; describe the difference or use two counters to model it.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Tempo and the speed of a beat
topics.description: Tempo describes the speed of the beat. A musician can make the same rhythm feel faster or slower by changing the tempo while preserving the order of its sounds.
topics.locator: PDF p. 12, Elements of Music: Expressive elements, Phase 1 > Music, Year 2
objectives: Explain or demonstrate tempo and the speed of a beat in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The tempo has increased.
misconceptions: A faster tempo necessarily means that the sounds are louder.
topics.question: A four-beat pattern is repeated with a faster pulse. What has changed?
topics.answer: The tempo has increased.
topics.explanation: The beats occur closer together in time; the sound pattern can remain in the same order.
hints: Listen for the spacing between beats.
What word describes the speed of a steady beat?
topics.activity: Tap four comfortable, evenly spaced beats twice, changing their speed on the second attempt, and describe which has the faster tempo.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Pitched and unpitched percussion
topics.description: Some percussion instruments produce a readily identifiable pitch, such as a tuned xylophone. Others are usually described as unpitched because they are not used to play a specific musical pitch, such as a shaker.
topics.locator: PDF p. 12–13, Elements of Music: Tone colour, Phase 1 > Music, Year 3
objectives: Explain or demonstrate pitched and unpitched percussion in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A tuned xylophone can play notes with identifiable pitches.
