misconceptions: All percussion instruments produce the same kind of pitch.
topics.question: Which could play a recognisable tune: a tuned xylophone or a shaker?
topics.answer: A tuned xylophone can play notes with identifiable pitches.
topics.explanation: Different bars of a tuned xylophone produce different identifiable notes; a shaker mainly produces an unpitched sound.
hints: Which instrument has tuned bars?
What does a tune need the player to change?
topics.activity: Look at credited pictures or recordings of a xylophone and a shaker; label which can play a sequence of identifiable notes.
materials: credited pictures or recordings of a xylophone and a shaker

topics.name: Musical call and response
topics.description: In call and response, one musical phrase is followed by another phrase that answers it. The response may copy or differ from the call, depending on the piece and tradition.
topics.locator: PDF p. 13, Elements of Music: Form/structure, Phase 1 > Music, Year 3
objectives: Explain or demonstrate musical call and response in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The pattern played by the group after the leader is the response.
misconceptions: Call and response requires everyone to play every sound at exactly the same time.
topics.question: A leader claps a short pattern and a group answers with another pattern. Which part is the response?
topics.answer: The pattern played by the group after the leader is the response.
topics.explanation: The response follows the call, making a musical exchange between the two parts.
hints: Which pattern is played first?
Who answers the first pattern?
topics.activity: Take turns tapping a two-beat call and a two-beat reply, or draw corresponding marks, then identify the order.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Grouping beats in threes and fours
topics.description: Metre groups beats into recurring patterns. A three-beat group can be felt as strong–weak–weak, while a four-beat group can have a strong first beat and a secondary emphasis on the third.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Elements of Music: Beat and rhythm, Phase 2 > Music, Year 4
objectives: Explain or demonstrate grouping beats in threes and fours in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A group of three beats.
misconceptions: Every piece of music groups its beats in fours.
topics.question: Which count fits a repeating strong–weak–weak pattern?
topics.answer: A group of three beats.
topics.explanation: The same emphasis returns after three counts, so each group has three beats.
hints: How many beats occur before the strong beat returns?
Count strong, weak, weak.
topics.activity: Mark three circles with one strong beat and then four circles with a strong first beat; tap either pattern or point to the circles.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: A five-note scale
topics.description: A pentatonic scale uses five different notes before the pattern repeats at the octave. One example is C–D–E–G–A; other five-note scales use different notes and intervals.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 2 > Music, Year 4
objectives: Explain or demonstrate a five-note scale in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Five: C, D, E, G and A.
misconceptions: Every pentatonic scale has exactly the same five note names.
topics.question: How many different notes appear before C returns in the pattern C–D–E–G–A–C?
topics.answer: Five: C, D, E, G and A.
topics.explanation: The last C repeats the starting note at another octave, so it is not a sixth different note.
hints: Count each different letter before the last C.
Does the final C introduce a new note name?
topics.activity: Write the example pattern, circle the five different notes and create a short sequence using any three of them; an instrument is optional.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: String length and pitch
topics.description: On a string instrument, shortening the vibrating length of the same string generally raises its pitch. The result also depends on the string and how the instrument is adjusted.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 2 > Music, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate string length and pitch in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The pitch rises.
misconceptions: Shortening a string always makes the note louder rather than changing pitch.
topics.question: A player presses a string so that a shorter section can vibrate. What generally happens to its pitch?
topics.answer: The pitch rises.
topics.explanation: A shorter vibrating section of the same string vibrates more rapidly under comparable conditions.
hints: Is the vibrating portion longer or shorter?
Does a higher pitch sound higher or louder?
topics.activity: Draw one long and one shortened vibrating string and label the expected pitch relationship; do not alter or overstretch an instrument.

topics.name: Note values in four-four time
topics.description: In 4/4 time, a quarter note represents one beat, a half note two beats and a whole note four beats; two eighth notes together take one beat. The time signature establishes the beat unit.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Elements of Music: Beat and rhythm, Phase 3 > Music, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate note values in four-four time in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Four beats.
misconceptions: A note's written value is the same as its pitch.
topics.question: How many beats do two half notes fill in a 4/4 bar?
topics.answer: Four beats.
topics.explanation: Each half note lasts two beats in this time signature, so two half notes fill a four-beat bar.
hints: How many beats is one half note worth here?
Add the durations of both notes.
topics.activity: Draw four beat boxes and fill them with either four quarter notes or two half notes, then compare their total duration.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Reading a four-four time signature
topics.description: A time signature organises beats into bars. In 4/4, the top number specifies four beats per bar and the bottom number identifies the quarter note as the beat unit.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Elements of Music: Beat and rhythm, Phase 3 > Music, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate reading a four-four time signature in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: There are four beats in each bar.
misconceptions: The upper number in a time signature tells a player how loudly to perform.
topics.question: What does the upper 4 in a 4/4 time signature indicate?
topics.answer: There are four beats in each bar.
topics.explanation: The top number counts the beats grouped into each bar in this signature.
hints: Look at the upper number.
What is counted within a bar?
topics.activity: Draw two four-beat bars using four marks in each, then label how many beats the upper number describes.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Sharps, flats and naturals
topics.description: In standard Western notation, a sharp raises a written note by a semitone, a flat lowers it by a semitone, and a natural cancels an applicable sharp or flat. Other musical traditions may use additional pitch distinctions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 3 > Music, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate sharps, flats and naturals in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: It becomes F sharp, one semitone higher than F natural.
misconceptions: A sharp symbol makes a note louder without changing its pitch.
topics.question: What happens to a written F when a sharp is applied?
topics.answer: It becomes F sharp, one semitone higher than F natural.
topics.explanation: A sharp changes the pitch upward by one semitone rather than changing its loudness.
hints: Does a sharp raise or lower a note?
What interval is a single semitone?
topics.activity: On a keyboard diagram, locate F and F sharp, then label the direction of the change without needing to play the notes.

topics.name: Soft and loud dynamic markings
topics.description: Dynamic markings describe relative loudness. In conventional notation p stands for piano, or soft, while f stands for forte, or loud; a performer interprets them in context.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Elements of Music: Expressive elements, Phase 3 > Music, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate soft and loud dynamic markings in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: It asks for a change from soft to loud.
misconceptions: The symbol p always means to play a piano instrument.
topics.question: A score changes from p to f. What change in loudness does it request?
topics.answer: It asks for a change from soft to loud.
topics.explanation: The markings identify relative dynamic levels, while the actual sound depends on the instrument and ensemble.
hints: Which letter means piano?
Does forte ask for soft or loud sound?
topics.activity: Mark a four-beat pattern p for the first two beats and f for the next two; point to the change or tap at comfortable volumes.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Gradual changes in dynamics
topics.description: A crescendo asks for sound to become gradually louder, and a decrescendo asks for it to become gradually softer. These changes concern dynamics rather than the speed of the beat.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Elements of Music: Expressive elements, Phase 3 > Music, Year 8
objectives: Explain or demonstrate gradual changes in dynamics in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A decrescendo.
misconceptions: A crescendo automatically means that the music must get faster.
topics.question: A sound grows gradually softer over four beats. Which dynamic change is this?
topics.answer: A decrescendo.
topics.explanation: The loudness decreases over time; the beat can stay at the same speed.
hints: Is the sound getting louder or softer?
Which term describes becoming gradually softer?
topics.activity: Draw a four-beat line and use an arrow or widening and narrowing marks to plan gradual changes in loudness, then demonstrate at a comfortable volume if suitable.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Ostinato as a repeating layer
topics.description: An ostinato is a short rhythmic or melodic pattern that repeats, often beneath another musical idea. It can provide continuity while a melody or other section changes.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Elements of Music: Form/structure, Phase 3 > Music, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate ostinato as a repeating layer in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: An ostinato.
misconceptions: A repeating pattern must stop whenever a different melody begins.
topics.question: A bass pattern repeats underneath several different sung phrases. What is the repeating pattern called?
topics.answer: An ostinato.
topics.explanation: The same short musical idea continues as a supporting layer while the phrases above it change.
hints: Which idea continues to return?
Is that idea rhythmic, melodic, or both?
topics.activity: Write a two-beat tapping pattern and repeat it four times while a partner speaks an unrelated short phrase, or draw the two layers.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: C, F and G major key signatures
topics.description: A key signature shows the sharps or flats normally used in a key. C major has none, F major has one flat on B, and G major has one sharp on F; further accidentals can still occur in a piece.
topics.locator: PDF p. 33, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 4 > Music, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate c, f and g major key signatures in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: F is sharpened to F sharp.
misconceptions: A key signature says every note in the piece must be sharpened.
topics.question: Which note is sharpened by the key signature of G major?
topics.answer: F is sharpened to F sharp.
topics.explanation: G major's key signature contains one sharp, placed on F.
hints: How many sharps are in G major?
Which note receives that sharp?
topics.activity: Write the key names C, F and G major and match them with no accidentals, B flat, or F sharp using a simple key-signature reference.

topics.name: Treble and bass clefs
topics.description: The clef assigns pitch names to positions on a staff. In treble clef the lines from bottom to top are E–G–B–D–F; in bass clef they are G–B–D–F–A.
topics.locator: PDF p. 33, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 4 > Music, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate treble and bass clefs in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: E.
misconceptions: A line on a staff always names the same note regardless of the clef.
topics.question: What note is on the bottom line of a treble staff?
topics.answer: E.
topics.explanation: The treble clef fixes the bottom line as E; the same visual position represents a different note with a bass clef.
hints: Identify the clef before naming the line.
Read the treble lines from the bottom upward.
topics.activity: Draw two five-line staves, label one treble and one bass, then label the bottom line of each using a reference.

topics.name: Dotted note duration
topics.description: A dot after a note adds half the note's original duration. In 4/4 time a dotted half note therefore lasts three beats: two beats plus one additional beat.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32, Elements of Music: Beat and rhythm, Phase 4 > Music, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate dotted note duration in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Three beats.
misconceptions: A dot after a note always doubles its duration.
topics.question: How many beats is a dotted half note worth in 4/4?
topics.answer: Three beats.
topics.explanation: A half note is two beats, and the dot adds half of two, which is one additional beat.
hints: How many beats is a half note in 4/4?
What is half of that value?
topics.activity: Draw three beat boxes to show two beats for a half note and the extra beat added by the dot, then compare with a plain half note.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: A tie joining the same pitch
topics.description: A tie joins two written notes of the same pitch so they are sustained as one combined duration. It is useful when the sound needs to continue across a bar line.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32, Elements of Music: Beat and rhythm, Phase 4 > Music, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate a tie joining the same pitch in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Two beats.
misconceptions: A tie asks a performer to strike both notes separately.
topics.question: Two quarter notes of the same pitch are joined by a tie in 4/4. How long is the sustained sound?
topics.answer: Two beats.
topics.explanation: The two one-beat durations are added, and the second note is not re-attacked.
hints: What is the duration of each quarter note?
Does a tie join the durations or instruct a separate attack?
topics.activity: Draw two beat boxes and connect identical note symbols with a curved tie, then indicate one continuous sound across both boxes.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Legato and staccato
topics.description: Articulation describes how notes are shaped and connected. Legato suggests smooth connection, while staccato suggests separated or detached notes.
topics.locator: PDF p. 33, Elements of Music: Expressive elements, Phase 4 > Music, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate legato and staccato in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Staccato.
misconceptions: Staccato and legato only describe how loud the music is.
topics.question: A performer plays each note distinctly separated. Which articulation is being used?
topics.answer: Staccato.
topics.explanation: The notes have audible separation rather than a smooth connection between them.
hints: Are the notes connected smoothly or detached?
Which term describes detached notes?
topics.activity: Draw four dots to represent separated notes and four linked curves to represent a smooth phrase; if appropriate, demonstrate both at a comfortable volume.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Relative major and minor scales
topics.description: Relative major and minor scales share a key signature but begin on different tonic notes. C major and A natural minor, for example, use the same key signature with different tonal centres.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 4 > Music, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate relative major and minor scales in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Neither has sharps or flats in its key signature.
misconceptions: Two scales with the same key signature must have the same tonic.
topics.question: What key signature do C major and its relative A natural minor share?
topics.answer: Neither has sharps or flats in its key signature.
topics.explanation: Their shared key signature does not make their tonic notes or musical character identical.
hints: Which major key is listed without sharps or flats?
Does sharing a key signature require the same starting note?
topics.activity: Write the notes C–D–E–F–G–A–B and reorder the same note names starting on A; mark each starting note.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Major and minor triad quality
topics.description: Major and minor triads each contain a root, a third and a fifth. Their third differs: C major uses C–E–G, while C minor uses C–E flat–G.
topics.locator: PDF p. 33, Elements of Music: Harmony, Phase 4 > Music, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate major and minor triad quality in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The third changes from E to E flat.
misconceptions: Major and minor triads always have different root notes.
topics.question: What changes between C major C–E–G and C minor C–E flat–G?
topics.answer: The third changes from E to E flat.
topics.explanation: The root C and fifth G remain the same; lowering the third changes the triad's quality.
hints: Compare the first and last notes of each triad.
Which middle note has changed?
topics.activity: Write both triads side by side and circle the changed note; play them only if a suitable instrument is available.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Compound metre in six-eight
topics.description: In 6/8 compound metre, six eighth-note subdivisions are commonly grouped as two main beats of three. This grouping differs from counting six equal accents.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32, Elements of Music: Beat and rhythm, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate compound metre in six-eight in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Two main beats, each divided into three eighth notes.
misconceptions: Six-eight always has six equally stressed main beats.
topics.question: How many main beats are commonly felt in one 6/8 bar when the eighth notes are grouped in threes?
topics.answer: Two main beats, each divided into three eighth notes.
topics.explanation: The six subdivisions form two groups of three rather than six equally accented main beats.
hints: Divide six subdivisions into equal groups of three.
How many groups result?
topics.activity: Write six dots and circle them in two groups of three; point to the first dot in each group as the main beat.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Monophonic and homophonic texture
topics.description: Monophonic texture has one melodic line without an independent accompaniment, even if several voices sing it in unison. Homophonic texture has a prominent melody supported by chords.
topics.locator: PDF p. 33, Elements of Music: Texture, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate monophonic and homophonic texture in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Homophonic texture.
misconceptions: Several singers in unison automatically create several independent melodic lines.
topics.question: A singer performs a melody while a piano supplies chords. Which texture does this example illustrate?
topics.answer: Homophonic texture.
topics.explanation: A principal melody is supported by chordal accompaniment, so it is more than a single unaccompanied line.
hints: Is there an accompaniment?
Does the accompaniment support the melody with chords?
topics.activity: Draw two diagrams: one line alone and one melody above chord blocks, then label the textures and explain one distinction.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Block and broken chords
topics.description: A block chord sounds its notes together. A broken chord presents the chord's notes separately in sequence, changing the accompaniment pattern while retaining the same set of notes.
topics.locator: PDF p. 33, Elements of Music: Texture, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate block and broken chords in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A broken chord.
misconceptions: A broken chord must use different notes from the corresponding block chord.
topics.question: C, E and G are played one after another instead of together. Which accompaniment pattern is this?
topics.answer: A broken chord.
topics.explanation: The chord tones are sounded in sequence rather than simultaneously.
hints: Do the three notes start together?
What is the term for notes of a chord played separately?
topics.activity: Write C–E–G vertically for a block chord and in a horizontal sequence for a broken chord, then compare the ordering.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Gradual tempo changes
topics.description: Accelerando directs a performer to become gradually faster; ritardando directs a gradual slowing. These tempo changes concern the spacing of beats, not necessarily their volume.
topics.locator: PDF p. 33, Elements of Music: Expressive elements, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate gradual tempo changes in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Gradually slow the tempo.
misconceptions: Ritardando is the same as gradually playing more quietly.
topics.question: What does ritardando ask a performer to do?
topics.answer: Gradually slow the tempo.
topics.explanation: The beats become farther apart over time; the performer can keep a similar dynamic level.
hints: Does the instruction concern speed or loudness?
Which term means gradually slowing down?
topics.activity: Draw five beat marks spaced progressively farther apart and label the change; compare them with five marks moving closer together.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Flashback in drama
topics.description: A flashback presents an earlier event within the current action. Performers can signal the shift in time through narration, movement, lighting or another agreed convention.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Constructing and Responding, Phase 3 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate flashback in drama in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A flashback.
misconceptions: All scenes in a drama must be presented in chronological order.
topics.question: A scene pauses and shows what happened the previous day. What convention is being used?
topics.answer: A flashback.
topics.explanation: The action moves to an earlier point in the story, giving the audience information about the past.
hints: Does the new scene happen earlier or later?
What term describes returning to an earlier event?
topics.activity: Outline a fictional present-day scene and a brief earlier event; add a safe, clear cue to show when the time changes.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Subtext and performance choices
topics.description: Subtext is what a character may think or feel beneath the words they say. Voice, pauses and movement can suggest subtext while allowing an audience to form its own interpretation.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30, Constructing, Phase 4 > Drama, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate subtext and performance choices in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The character may be upset or hesitant despite saying they are fine.
misconceptions: A character's words always reveal every thought or feeling directly.
topics.question: A character says “Fine” while looking away and pausing. What might the performance suggest?
topics.answer: The character may be upset or hesitant despite saying they are fine.
topics.explanation: The pause and gaze contrast with the spoken words, offering evidence for a possible underlying feeling.
hints: What do the words say?
What different clue comes from the pause or movement?
topics.activity: Write a two-line fictional exchange and annotate two contrasting ways to deliver one line; explain the different possible subtexts.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Movement-focused theatre
topics.description: Physical theatre can communicate a story through movement, gesture and the use of space. Spoken language, objects and sound may also be used, depending on the work and its makers.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30, Constructing, Phase 4 > Drama, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate movement-focused theatre in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They could coordinate body movement and changes of balance to suggest the rocking.
misconceptions: A dramatic story can be told only through spoken dialogue.
topics.question: How might a group show that an imaginary boat is rocking without building a boat set?
topics.answer: They could coordinate body movement and changes of balance to suggest the rocking.
topics.explanation: Shared movement can represent the imagined action and help an audience understand the situation.
hints: What would people on a rocking boat do with their bodies?
How could the group move together to suggest that action?
topics.activity: Create or sketch three safe body positions suggesting a fictional journey, then identify the clue each position gives an audience.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Dance purpose and performance setting
topics.description: Dance can be made for many purposes, including community participation, celebration and performance for an audience. A particular work's purpose and conventions depend on its makers and context, and these purposes can overlap.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Observing, Performing and Responding, Phase 4 > Dance, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate dance purpose and performance setting in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Consider each dance's makers, occasion and intended participants or audience.
misconceptions: Every dance made by a community has the same purpose and protocols.
topics.question: A community dance and a theatre piece both include group movement. What should a viewer consider before interpreting them?
topics.answer: Consider each dance's makers, occasion and intended participants or audience.
topics.explanation: Similar movements can serve different purposes, so an interpretation needs evidence about each work's context.
hints: Who made or participates in each dance?
What information explains the occasion or audience?
topics.activity: Compare two credited descriptions of dance events and record one purpose and one question for each source, without copying culturally significant movements.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Simple and overlapping canon
topics.description: In a simple canon one dancer may finish a phrase before the next begins; in an overlapping canon another dancer starts while the first is still moving. Both use a staggered repetition.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Exploring and Creating, Phase 4 > Dance, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate simple and overlapping canon in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: An overlapping canon.
misconceptions: Canon always requires the first performer to finish before the next begins.
topics.question: A second dancer starts the same phrase while the first dancer is still performing it. Which canon is this?
topics.answer: An overlapping canon.
topics.explanation: The staggered entries overlap in time rather than waiting for the first phrase to finish.
hints: Has the first dancer finished before the second starts?
Are both phrases occurring during part of the same time?
topics.activity: Use two rows of four boxes to plan a phrase and its delayed entry; shade where the two rows overlap.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Three-dimensional form
topics.description: A three-dimensional form has height, width and depth. It can be a physical object such as a sculpture, or it can be suggested on a flat surface through shading and perspective.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Making and Creating, Phase 2 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate three-dimensional form in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: It has height, width and depth.
misconceptions: A form is three-dimensional only if it is made from expensive materials.
topics.question: A cardboard sculpture can be viewed from the front, side and above. What quality makes it three-dimensional?
topics.answer: It has height, width and depth.
topics.explanation: The object occupies space in three dimensions rather than existing only as a flat outline.
hints: Can the object be viewed from different sides?
What dimension extends from front to back?
topics.activity: Fold a safe scrap-paper shape so it stands, or draw its front and side views, then name its height, width and depth.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Scale and balance in composition
topics.description: Scale is the relative size of visual elements; balance concerns how their visual weight is distributed. A composition can be balanced without placing identical objects on both sides.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Making and Creating, Phase 3 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate scale and balance in composition in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The artist could change the sizes, contrast or positions of the shapes.
misconceptions: A balanced composition must always be perfectly symmetrical.
topics.question: A large dark shape is placed opposite several smaller shapes. What could the artist adjust to change the balance?
topics.answer: The artist could change the sizes, contrast or positions of the shapes.
topics.explanation: Visual balance depends on the combined weight and arrangement of elements, not only their number.
hints: Which side has the larger dark shape?
How could the smaller shapes be arranged to counter its visual weight?
topics.activity: Arrange paper shapes in two different compositions, changing only size or placement, and describe how the balance changes.
materials: paper and pencil, or an accessible equivalent

topics.name: Actions in a waiata context
topics.description: Some waiata are accompanied by particular movements or gestures that can contribute to their meaning. The actions and appropriate way to participate depend on the specific waiata and community, so guidance from a knowledgeable teacher or relevant community is important.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Dance Contexts and Exploring and Creating, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate actions in a waiata context in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Ask a knowledgeable teacher or relevant community about the particular waiata and appropriate actions.
misconceptions: Every waiata uses the same actions and can be treated as a generic template.
topics.question: A class wants to learn the actions for a named waiata. What should it do before inventing movements?
topics.answer: Ask a knowledgeable teacher or relevant community about the particular waiata and appropriate actions.
topics.explanation: A named waiata can have its own meaning and established actions, which should not be assumed from an unrelated example.
hints: Is every waiata identical?
Who can explain the actions and context of this particular waiata?
topics.activity: With a teacher-provided, appropriately credited example, identify a movement and ask how its meaning or use was explained; learners may observe without performing.
materials: a teacher-provided, attributed example and explanation

topics.name: Geometric and organic shapes
topics.description: Geometric shapes include regular forms such as circles and triangles; organic shapes can have freer or irregular outlines associated with natural forms. Artists can combine both kinds of shape in a picture.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Making and Creating: Elements, Phase 1 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate geometric and organic shapes in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The circle is a geometric shape; the leaf outline is an example of an organic shape.
misconceptions: Every shape found in an artwork must be a perfect geometric shape.
topics.question: Which shape is geometric: a circle or a freely drawn leaf outline?
topics.answer: The circle is a geometric shape; the leaf outline is an example of an organic shape.
topics.explanation: The circle is a regular named shape, while the drawn leaf can have a less regular outline.
hints: Which shape has a familiar mathematical name?
Which outline is free-form or irregular?
topics.activity: Draw one circle, one triangle and one leaf-like outline, then use two of them in a simple imaginary composition.

topics.name: Adapting a story for drama
topics.description: A stage adaptation makes choices about scenes, characters and dialogue from a particular source story. When a story belongs to a living community, creators should identify the source and seek appropriate guidance on how it may be shared or adapted.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Responding: Narrative plays, Phase 2 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate adapting a story for drama in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Identify the storyteller or source and ask the relevant community about appropriate sharing and adaptation.
misconceptions: A story may be changed and performed in any way simply because it was heard in public.
topics.question: A group wants to adapt a story told by a local community. What should it establish before changing it?
topics.answer: Identify the storyteller or source and ask the relevant community about appropriate sharing and adaptation.
topics.explanation: Knowing the source and seeking guidance helps the group respect the story's context and the people connected to it.
hints: Who is responsible for the story or version?
Who could explain whether the proposed use is appropriate?
topics.activity: Use a fictional permission scenario to list a credited source, a proposed change and one question for the relevant storyteller; do not reproduce a protected story.

topics.name: Materials in the Bayin classification
topics.description: One traditional Chinese instrument classification, Bayin, groups instruments according to materials such as bamboo, silk, stone and metal. A classification describes a particular system; it does not imply that all instruments in a culture are used in the same way.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Elements of Music: Tone colour, Phase 3 > Music, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate materials in the bayin classification in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Bamboo.
misconceptions: Every culture must group instruments using the same categories.
topics.question: In this material-based classification, which material group would be relevant to a bamboo instrument?
topics.answer: Bamboo.
topics.explanation: Bayin names material groups, so an instrument classified by bamboo is associated with that material group.
hints: Does this system classify by material or by loudness?
What material is named in the example?
topics.activity: Using a credited description of the Bayin system, match three listed materials with their names and write one question about a specific instrument and maker.
materials: a credited description of Bayin and paper

topics.name: Examples of taonga pūoro
topics.description: Taonga pūoro encompass diverse Māori instruments and associated knowledge. A kōauau is an example of a flute, while a pūtātara is a shell trumpet; the context and appropriate use of a particular instrument should be learned from attributed Māori sources and practitioners.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Elements of Music: Tone colour, Phase 3 > Music, Year 7
objectives: Explain or demonstrate examples of taonga pūoro in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Kōauau is an example of a flute; pūtātara is a shell trumpet.
misconceptions: All taonga pūoro are the same instrument and have one universal use.
topics.question: Which example is a flute: kōauau or pūtātara?
topics.answer: Kōauau is an example of a flute; pūtātara is a shell trumpet.
topics.explanation: The two names refer to different instruments, and each may have particular histories and contexts explained by knowledgeable practitioners.
hints: Which name refers to the flute in the description?
Does one instrument name stand for every taonga pūoro?
topics.activity: Use an attributed, appropriate Māori source to match these two names to their instrument types and record the source; do not make or imitate instruments without guidance.
materials: an attributed Māori source on taonga pūoro

topics.name: Musical tradition and innovation
topics.description: Musicians may draw on established practices while developing new sounds, instruments or forms. A particular work's relationship to a tradition should be studied through the artist's own account and other reliable, attributed sources.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32, Music Contexts and Listening and Responding, Phase 4 > Music; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate musical tradition and innovation in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Ask how the composer describes the instrument's role and the reasons for combining it with electronic sound.
misconceptions: A work cannot contain both a traditional practice and an innovative choice.
topics.question: A credited composer combines an established instrument with electronic sounds. What question could help explain that choice?
topics.answer: Ask how the composer describes the instrument's role and the reasons for combining it with electronic sound.
topics.explanation: The maker's account and the work's context help explain how a specific combination relates to tradition and innovation.
hints: Who made the work?
What can that maker or another reliable source say about the combination?
topics.activity: Choose a teacher-provided credited work description, list one established and one newer sound-making choice, and cite a source that explains the combination.
materials: a credited work description or artist account

topics.name: Documentary photography and context
topics.description: Documentary photography can use framing, viewpoint and other choices to represent an event or social issue. Viewers should consider who made an image, what it includes or leaves out, and how the people shown were represented.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Making and Creating: Visual arts conventions, Phase 4 > Visual Arts, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate documentary photography and context in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The framing selects part of the event, so additional attributed information can help explain what is outside the image.
misconceptions: A photograph automatically shows every relevant aspect of an event.
topics.question: A photograph of a community event shows only one small part of the crowd. Why should a viewer seek more context?
topics.answer: The framing selects part of the event, so additional attributed information can help explain what is outside the image.
topics.explanation: Every photograph presents a particular viewpoint and selection rather than the whole event from every perspective.
hints: What is visible inside the frame?
What might a viewer need to know about what is outside it?
topics.activity: Analyse a teacher-provided credited photograph or a fictional sketch, label two framing choices and write one question about its context; do not photograph other people without permission.
materials: a credited photograph or fictional sketch and paper

topics.name: Responding to movement cues
topics.description: A dance group can use agreed visual or sound cues to begin, pause and finish together. Keeping an appropriate distance and allowing different ways to respond helps participants move safely.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Observing, Performing and Responding, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate responding to movement cues in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The dancers pause their movements while maintaining a comfortable position.
misconceptions: A group cue has no role in coordinating a dance.
topics.question: A group agrees to freeze when the leader raises a hand. What should happen at the cue?
topics.answer: The dancers pause their movements while maintaining a comfortable position.
topics.explanation: The shared signal coordinates the group and can create a clear moment of stillness.
hints: What action has the group agreed to?
Does the raised hand signal more movement or a pause?
topics.activity: Practise two fictional visual cues for beginning and pausing a comfortable seated or standing movement, leaving enough room for everyone.
materials: clear space or a seated equivalent

topics.name: Creating movement from a stimulus
topics.description: An image, sound or observation can inspire movement. Dancers choose features such as direction, shape or speed to develop an idea without needing to imitate a real animal or person exactly.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Exploring and Creating, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate creating movement from a stimulus in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The observed drifting leaf was the stimulus.
misconceptions: A dance idea can only come from copying an existing dance.
topics.question: A dancer sees a leaf drifting down and creates a slow curved hand movement. What was the stimulus?
topics.answer: The observed drifting leaf was the stimulus.
topics.explanation: The leaf provided an idea; the dancer chose how to translate it into a movement.
hints: What did the dancer observe first?
Which movement quality was chosen in response?
topics.activity: Use a drawing of rain or a leaf to choose one comfortable movement quality, then explain the connection; drawing the movement is also an option.
materials: an imaginary or drawn natural scene

topics.name: Hot-seating a fictional character
topics.description: Hot-seating is a drama convention in which a participant answers questions while in a fictional role. The activity can reveal a character's viewpoint and can be paused or exited by agreement.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Constructing: Drama conventions, Phase 2 > Drama, Year 4
objectives: Explain or demonstrate hot-seating a fictional character in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Hot-seating.
misconceptions: A performer in role must reveal their own private experiences.
topics.question: A fictional explorer answers classmates' questions as that character. What convention is being used?
topics.answer: Hot-seating.
topics.explanation: The participant responds from the imagined character's viewpoint rather than speaking as themselves.
hints: Who is answering the questions?
Are they answering as themselves or as the imagined character?
topics.activity: Write two non-personal questions for a fictional character and two possible in-role answers; performing aloud is optional.

topics.name: Status between fictional characters
topics.description: Status describes a character's relative power or position in a particular dramatic situation. It can shift as circumstances change and can be suggested through dialogue, posture and use of space.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Constructing: Character features, Phase 2 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate status between fictional characters in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The characters' relative status and how it changes when the order is challenged.
misconceptions: A character's status must remain identical in every scene.
topics.question: A fictional captain gives an order that a crew member can challenge. What dramatic relationship could the scene explore?
topics.answer: The characters' relative status and how it changes when the order is challenged.
topics.explanation: The captain has a position of authority, while the response can show how that authority is negotiated in the scene.
hints: Who initially gives the instruction?
How might the other character's response change the relationship?
topics.activity: Outline a fictional scene with two characters and one change in who makes a decision; identify a line or action that signals the change.

topics.name: Mime and imagined objects
topics.description: Mime uses controlled movement and gesture to suggest an action or object without relying on the real object. Clear size, weight and timing can help an audience understand the imagined situation.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Constructing: Techniques and conventions, Phase 3 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate mime and imagined objects in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: They suggest that the imagined box is heavy.
misconceptions: Mime can only communicate meaning if the real object is present.
topics.question: A performer pretends to lift a heavy box slowly with both hands. What do the movement choices suggest?
topics.answer: They suggest that the imagined box is heavy.
topics.explanation: The slow, effortful movement and two-handed grip give visual clues about the imaginary object's weight.
hints: What object is being imagined?
How do the performer's speed and hands suggest its weight?
topics.activity: Describe or demonstrate safely lifting an imaginary light object and then a heavy one; ask an observer which movement clues they noticed.
materials: clear space or a seated equivalent

topics.name: Symmetry in dance shapes
topics.description: A symmetrical body shape or group formation has corresponding parts arranged around an imagined line; an asymmetrical shape has different arrangements on each side. Either choice can be used intentionally in a dance.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Exploring and Creating: Body shapes and formations, Phase 4 > Dance, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate symmetry in dance shapes in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: It shows symmetry in the arm positions.
misconceptions: An asymmetrical shape is always a mistake.
topics.question: A dancer holds both arms at matching heights on either side. What quality does the shape show?
topics.answer: It shows symmetry in the arm positions.
topics.explanation: The two sides correspond across an imagined central line.
hints: Compare the height of the left and right arms.
Do the two sides match or differ?
topics.activity: Sketch one symmetrical and one asymmetrical arm shape, or explore comfortable seated or standing versions without forcing a position.
materials: paper and pencil or clear space

topics.name: Ensemble entrances and exits
topics.description: Dancers coordinate entrances, exits, spacing and timing so that a group composition can be performed clearly and safely. Cues should account for different ways performers can move and perceive signals.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Observing, Performing and Responding: Ensemble skills, Phase 4 > Dance, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate ensemble entrances and exits in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A shared entrance cue and a route that keeps appropriate space between performers.
misconceptions: An entrance only concerns costume and has nothing to do with timing or space.
topics.question: A group changes formation when two dancers enter. What should it plan?
topics.answer: A shared entrance cue and a route that keeps appropriate space between performers.
topics.explanation: Planning timing and pathways helps the new dancers join the formation without crowding others.
hints: When will the new dancers begin?
Where can they move while keeping a safe distance?
topics.activity: Use counters on a paper stage to plan two entrances and an exit, marking a cue and safe routes; physical performance is optional.

topics.name: Repeating visual elements
topics.description: A visual pattern can be made by repeating shapes, lines, colours or marks in an arrangement. A change in the repeated element can create a new rhythm or point of interest.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Making and Creating: Mark-making and pattern, Phase 1 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate repeating visual elements in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The alternating circle-and-triangle sequence repeats.
misconceptions: A pattern requires every mark to be completely different.
topics.question: A picture repeats circle, triangle, circle, triangle. What creates the pattern?
topics.answer: The alternating circle-and-triangle sequence repeats.
topics.explanation: The repeated order allows a viewer to anticipate what may come next.
hints: Which two shapes appear more than once?
What order do they repeat in?
topics.activity: Use simple self-created shapes to draw two repetitions, then change one shape and describe the effect; avoid copying a culturally significant motif.

topics.name: Warm and cool colour choices
topics.description: Artists often group colours such as red and orange as warm, and blue and green as cool. These are useful descriptive relationships rather than fixed emotional meanings, and the effect depends on the surrounding colours and context.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Making and Creating: Colour theory, Phase 2 > Visual Arts; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate warm and cool colour choices in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Blue.
misconceptions: A particular colour always produces the same emotion for every viewer.
topics.question: Which colour from a red, orange and blue set is commonly described as cool?
topics.answer: Blue.
topics.explanation: Blue is commonly placed among cool colours, while red and orange are commonly described as warm.
hints: Which colour is associated with the cool side of a colour wheel?
Compare blue with the red and orange examples.
topics.activity: Divide a page into two areas and arrange fictional warm and cool colour swatches; describe a possible mood without assuming every viewer responds alike.
materials: paper and coloured pencils or a colour wheel

topics.name: Perspective and relative size
topics.description: Artists can suggest depth on a flat surface by changing the relative size of similar objects. In many views, objects of similar actual size appear smaller when farther away, although the effect depends on viewpoint.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Making and Creating: Perspective, Phase 4 > Visual Arts, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate perspective and relative size in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: It can suggest that the smaller tree is farther away.
misconceptions: An object drawn smaller must always represent an object that is smaller in real life.
topics.question: A drawing shows two similar trees, with the farther tree drawn smaller. What idea can that choice suggest?
topics.answer: It can suggest that the smaller tree is farther away.
topics.explanation: The change in size provides a depth cue when the viewer understands the objects to be of similar actual size.
hints: Are the trees meant to be similar in real size?
Which one appears farther away?
topics.activity: Draw a path with two similar imaginary objects at different sizes, then label the nearer and farther one and explain the clue.

topics.name: Repeating marks in printmaking
topics.description: Printmaking can repeat an image or mark by transferring it from a surface. Artists can change the arrangement, colour or spacing between impressions to create a pattern.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Making and Creating: Printmaking, Phase 4 > Visual Arts, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate repeating marks in printmaking in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Repetition of a transferred mark.
misconceptions: Every printed impression must be an entirely different image.
topics.question: An artist presses the same simple shape onto paper several times. What printmaking feature are they exploring?
topics.answer: Repetition of a transferred mark.
topics.explanation: The same source shape makes several related impressions, while their arrangement can still vary.
hints: How many times is the shape used?
What remains recognisable in each impression?
topics.activity: Use a safe pre-cut sponge or draw a stamp shape, plan three impressions and change their spacing; avoid sharp carving tools and culturally significant designs.
materials: paper and a safe pre-cut sponge or pencil

topics.name: Layering and blending paint
topics.description: Painting can use layers and blended colours to build visual effects. An artist can test how an added layer changes colour or texture before deciding whether it supports the intended image.
topics.locator: PDF p. 35, Making and Creating: Painting, Phase 4 > Visual Arts, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate layering and blending paint in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Layering paint and observing the resulting colour.
misconceptions: Adding a layer can never change the appearance of a colour underneath.
topics.question: An artist adds a thin layer of blue over a dry yellow area to test a new effect. What process are they exploring?
topics.answer: Layering paint and observing the resulting colour.
topics.explanation: A new layer changes the appearance of the area beneath it, with results depending on the materials and their opacity.
hints: Is the new colour placed beside or over the earlier layer?
What can the artist compare before and after adding it?
topics.activity: On scrap paper, compare a single colour patch with a second patch containing an additional layer, or use translucent digital shapes; record one visible difference.
materials: scrap paper and suitable paints or a digital equivalent

topics.name: An octave between matching note names
topics.description: An octave is the interval between a pitch and the next higher or lower pitch with the same note name and accidental. For example, C natural and the next higher C natural have the same note name at different pitch heights.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 2 > Music, Year 4
objectives: Explain or demonstrate an octave between matching note names in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: An octave.
misconceptions: Two notes an octave apart always sound at the same pitch height.
topics.question: What interval separates one C from the next higher C?
topics.answer: An octave.
topics.explanation: The note name repeats at a higher pitch after the intervening note names.
hints: Do the two notes have the same letter name?
What is the name of the interval between them?
topics.activity: Write C–D–E–F–G–A–B–C and mark the two Cs; a keyboard diagram is optional.
materials: paper and pencil, with an optional keyboard diagram

topics.name: Sounds in harmony
topics.description: Harmony can occur when two or more different pitches sound together. A chord is one way to organise pitches played simultaneously, often to support a melody.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Elements of Music: Harmony, Phase 2 > Music, Year 4
objectives: Explain or demonstrate sounds in harmony in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Harmony.
misconceptions: Harmony requires two notes to be played at different times.
topics.question: Two different notes sound at the same time. What musical feature can they create?
topics.answer: Harmony.
topics.explanation: The pitches are heard together rather than as a sequence of separate single notes.
hints: Are the notes sounding one after another or together?
What term describes pitches heard together?
topics.activity: Draw two note lines stacked at the same time position, then compare them with two notes drawn one after another; an instrument is optional.

topics.name: Naming interval numbers
topics.description: An interval describes the distance between two pitches. To name its number using note letters, count both the starting and ending note; C to E is a third because C, D and E are three letter positions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 3 > Music, Year 8
objectives: Explain or demonstrate naming interval numbers in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A third.
misconceptions: An interval number is found by counting only the notes between the endpoints.
topics.question: What numbered interval is C to E?
topics.answer: A third.
topics.explanation: Counting C, D and E inclusively gives three note-letter positions; the quality of an interval requires additional information.
hints: Count the starting note as one.
How many letter names are there from C through E?
topics.activity: Write C–D–E–F–G and circle the endpoints C and E, then count all included letters; do not assume the interval quality from the number alone.
materials: paper and pencil or a staff diagram

topics.name: Scale degrees and the tonic
topics.description: Scale degrees number the ordered notes of a scale. The first degree is the tonic; the matching note at the next octave can be counted as the eighth degree when including the octave.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 3 > Music, Year 8
objectives: Explain or demonstrate scale degrees and the tonic in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: C.
misconceptions: The tonic is always the loudest note in a piece.
topics.question: In a C major scale, which note is scale degree one and the tonic?
topics.answer: C.
topics.explanation: C begins the C major scale and therefore names its first scale degree.
hints: Write the scale starting on C.
Which note comes first?
topics.activity: Write C–D–E–F–G–A–B–C, number the notes from one to eight and label the tonic.

topics.name: Intro and outro in a song
topics.description: An introduction can establish the opening of a song, while an outro provides a closing section. A song may also use verses, choruses and other sections in a chosen order.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Elements of Music: Form/structure, Phase 3 > Music, Year 8
objectives: Explain or demonstrate intro and outro in a song in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The outro.
misconceptions: Every song must have exactly the same order of sections.
topics.question: Which section is commonly used to close a song: intro or outro?
topics.answer: The outro.
topics.explanation: An outro occurs at the end, while an intro occurs at the beginning.
hints: Which word refers to an ending?
Does the introduction come before or after the main song?
topics.activity: Arrange fictional section cards labelled intro, verse, chorus and outro in one possible order, then identify the first and last sections.
materials: paper and pencil or fictional section cards

topics.name: Tonic and dominant chords
topics.description: In a major key, chord I is built on the first scale degree and chord V on the fifth. In C major, C–E–G is chord I and G–B–D is chord V; moving from V to I can create a sense of resolution.
topics.locator: PDF p. 34, Elements of Music: Harmony, Phase 4 > Music, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate tonic and dominant chords in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: G–B–D, the dominant or V chord.
misconceptions: The dominant chord is always the same chord as the tonic chord.
topics.question: In C major, which chord is built on the fifth scale degree: C–E–G or G–B–D?
topics.answer: G–B–D, the dominant or V chord.
topics.explanation: G is the fifth note of the C major scale, so a triad built on G is the dominant chord.
hints: Count from C up to the fifth scale degree.
Which chord begins on G?
topics.activity: Write the C major scale and circle degrees one and five, then match C–E–G and G–B–D to I and V.

topics.name: The role of a bass line
topics.description: A bass line is a sequence of low notes that can outline the harmony and support the musical texture. Its exact rhythm and notes depend on the piece and arrangement.
topics.locator: PDF p. 34, Elements of Music: Harmony, Phase 4 > Music, Year 9
objectives: Explain or demonstrate the role of a bass line in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A bass line.
misconceptions: The bass line is always the highest melody in a piece.
topics.question: A low instrument plays changing notes beneath a melody to outline the chords. What is that part commonly called?
topics.answer: A bass line.
topics.explanation: The low sequence provides a supporting line related to the harmony beneath the melody.
hints: Which layer uses the lowest notes?
What does that line help outline?
topics.activity: Draw a high melody line above a lower line on a fictional timeline and describe one role of the lower part; listening is optional.

topics.name: Harmonic minor and the seventh degree
topics.description: A harmonic minor scale raises the seventh degree of the corresponding natural minor scale. In A minor, G in the natural minor form becomes G sharp in the harmonic minor form.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32–33, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate harmonic minor and the seventh degree in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: G is raised to G sharp.
misconceptions: Harmonic minor raises every note of a natural minor scale.
topics.question: Which note changes when A natural minor becomes A harmonic minor?
topics.answer: G is raised to G sharp.
topics.explanation: G is the seventh degree of the A natural minor scale, and the harmonic minor form raises it by a semitone.
hints: List A–B–C–D–E–F–G.
Which note is seventh, and what happens to it?
topics.activity: Write the A natural minor notes and replace the seventh note with its raised form, then label the change.

topics.name: Neighbouring keys on the Circle of Fifths
topics.description: The Circle of Fifths organises keys by intervals of a fifth. Around C major, G major is a fifth above and has one sharp; F major is a fifth below and has one flat.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate neighbouring keys on the circle of fifths in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: G major adds one sharp, F sharp.
misconceptions: Neighbouring major keys always have completely unrelated key signatures.
topics.question: How does G major's key signature differ from C major's?
topics.answer: G major adds one sharp, F sharp.
topics.explanation: C major has no sharps or flats in its key signature, while neighbouring G major has one sharp.
hints: What is the key signature of C major?
Which single sharp appears in G major?
topics.activity: Draw C in the centre of a small three-key diagram with G and F as neighbouring examples; label their key signatures using a reference.

topics.name: Repeat marks in notation
topics.description: Repeat marks tell a performer to return to an earlier section of written music and play it again as indicated. They can communicate a repeated structure without writing every note twice.
topics.locator: PDF p. 34, Elements of Music: Form/structure, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate repeat marks in notation in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Return to the indicated earlier point and repeat the passage.
misconceptions: A repeat mark means the performer should skip the passage entirely.
topics.question: A passage ends with a repeat sign. What does that sign tell a performer?
topics.answer: Return to the indicated earlier point and repeat the passage.
topics.explanation: The symbol is a structural instruction governing how the written section is performed.
hints: Is the sign about loudness or the order of sections?
What does repeating a passage mean?
topics.activity: Draw a short fictional sequence A followed by a repeat instruction and write the resulting order as A–A; a standard notation reference can be used for the sign.

topics.name: Equalisation and tone colour
topics.description: Equalisation, or EQ, changes the relative level of selected frequency ranges in an audio signal. A producer can use it to shape tone colour; the result depends on the sound, settings and listening context.
topics.locator: PDF p. 34, Music Technology (optional): Sound production, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate equalisation and tone colour in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The recording's tone colour may become less bright.
misconceptions: EQ automatically changes the notes in a recorded melody.
topics.question: If a producer reduces high frequencies on a recording, what quality might change?
topics.answer: The recording's tone colour may become less bright.
topics.explanation: Changing the balance of frequencies alters the sound's spectrum rather than rewriting the melody's notes.
hints: Does EQ act on frequency ranges or the spelling of lyrics?
What might happen if high frequencies are reduced?
topics.activity: On a fictional graph, lower a high-frequency band and describe one possible audible effect; software is optional and listening volume should remain comfortable.
materials: paper and a fictional frequency graph

topics.name: Thought-tracking in drama
topics.description: Thought-tracking is a convention in which a fictional character's thoughts are spoken or otherwise shared while the dramatic action pauses. The thoughts are invented for the role, so no one needs to disclose personal feelings.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Constructing: Drama conventions, Phase 1 > Drama, Year 3
objectives: Explain or demonstrate thought-tracking in drama in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Thought-tracking.
misconceptions: Thought-tracking requires the performer to reveal what they personally feel.
topics.question: A fictional character freezes, and an actor says what that character might be thinking. Which convention is this?
topics.answer: Thought-tracking.
topics.explanation: The action is paused while the performer shares an imagined thought belonging to the character.
hints: Whose thought is being shared?
What happens to the action while that thought is expressed?
topics.activity: Draw a fictional character in a frozen scene and add one invented thought in a speech bubble; speaking or performing is optional.

topics.name: Split stage and simultaneous scenes
topics.description: Split stage is a convention that represents two places or scenes in different parts of the performance space. Performers can use focus and timing to help an audience follow the separate actions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 23, Constructing: Conventions, Phase 3 > Drama; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate split stage and simultaneous scenes in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Split stage.
misconceptions: Every part of a stage must represent the same location at all times.
topics.question: A stage shows one group at a station and another group at home at the same time. What convention is being used?
topics.answer: Split stage.
topics.explanation: Separate areas represent different locations within the same performance space.
hints: How many places are represented?
Are the places shown in one shared performance space?
topics.activity: Draw a rectangular stage divided into two fictional locations, add one action in each and indicate where the audience should look first.

topics.name: Positive and negative space in dance
topics.description: In dance, positive space includes the space occupied by a dancer's body; negative space is the space around or between body parts and performers. Choreographers can notice both when choosing shapes and relationships.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Exploring and Creating: Space, Phase 3 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate positive and negative space in dance in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Negative space.
misconceptions: Only the body matters when describing space in a dance shape.
topics.question: A dancer curves both arms to make an opening in front of their body. What is the opening an example of?
topics.answer: Negative space.
topics.explanation: The opening is an area of space framed by, but not occupied by, the dancer's body.
hints: Does the opening contain the dancer's arm?
Is it space around or between body parts?
topics.activity: Draw a simple figure with curved arms and colour the space framed by them, or form a comfortable shape with a seated option.
materials: paper and pencil or comfortable clear space

topics.name: Responding to a dance performance
topics.description: An audience can notice movement, timing and use of space, then describe what it saw. Appropriate audience responses depend on the performance and community; a teacher or host can explain local expectations.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9–10, Observing, Performing and Responding, Phase 1 > Dance; broad phase-level search scope
objectives: Explain or demonstrate responding to a dance performance in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The dancers first moved together and later used different timing.
misconceptions: A viewer must assign the same meaning to every dance movement.
topics.question: A viewer notices dancers begin together and later move at different times. What evidence could the viewer mention?
topics.answer: The dancers first moved together and later used different timing.
topics.explanation: The answer describes observable choices before interpreting their effect, while respecting the performance's context.
hints: What changed in the dancers' timing?
Can the viewer describe the change without assuming what it means?
topics.activity: Using a teacher-provided credited performance description or a fictional sequence, identify one movement detail and one question about appropriate audience response.
materials: credited performance description or fictional sequence

topics.name: Graphic notation and a key
topics.description: Graphic notation uses agreed marks or images to represent sounds. A key explains what each mark means, so another musician can interpret the intended sound even if the marks are not standard staff notation.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Elements of Music: Pitch and graphic notation, Phase 2 > Music, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate graphic notation and a key in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: As one tap, according to the key.
misconceptions: Only five-line staff notation can communicate a musical idea.
topics.question: A notation key says a dot means one tap and a dash means one long sound. How should a dot be performed?
topics.answer: As one tap, according to the key.
topics.explanation: The meaning comes from the shared key, which connects each visual mark to a sound.
hints: Find the dot in the key.
What sound has the creator assigned to it?
topics.activity: Invent two symbols and a short key, write a four-symbol pattern and ask another person to interpret it; pointing is an accessible alternative to tapping.

topics.name: Composing a soundscape
topics.description: A soundscape combines chosen sounds and silences to suggest a place, event or idea. A composer can plan which sounds occur together, repeat or change over time.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Improvising and Composing: Soundscape, Phase 2 > Music, Year 4
objectives: Explain or demonstrate composing a soundscape in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: A soundscape representing the imagined garden.
misconceptions: A composition needs written lyrics before it can suggest a place.
topics.question: A group chooses soft rustling, tapping and a pause to suggest a windy garden. What have they created?
topics.answer: A soundscape representing the imagined garden.
topics.explanation: The selected sounds and silence are organised to evoke an idea for listeners.
hints: What idea do the sounds represent?
Were the sounds selected and arranged for that purpose?
topics.activity: Plan a fictional journey with three sounds and one pause, using a simple written sequence; make sounds gently or communicate them visually.
materials: paper and pencil or optional safe sound sources

topics.name: Singing in unison and in parts
topics.description: In unison, performers sing or play the same musical line together. In two-part harmony, two different lines sound at the same time and are coordinated as an ensemble.
topics.locator: PDF p. 18, Performing: Unison and harmony, Phase 2 > Music, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate singing in unison and in parts in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Two-part harmony.
misconceptions: Two-part harmony means one group sings and the other must remain silent.
topics.question: Two groups sing different notes at the same time to support the same song. Which arrangement are they exploring?
topics.answer: Two-part harmony.
topics.explanation: The two groups perform different coordinated pitches rather than the same line in unison.
hints: Are the two groups singing the same line?
Do the different parts sound together?
topics.activity: Draw two rows of coloured marks to represent two coordinated parts; learners may listen or point instead of singing.
materials: paper and coloured pencils or visual marks

topics.name: How a brass instrument makes sound
topics.description: In many brass instruments, such as trumpets and trombones, the player's vibrating lips start a vibration of air in the instrument. Instrument families are classified by how they produce sound, not solely by their colour or appearance.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Elements of Music: Tone colour, Phase 2 > Music, Year 5
objectives: Explain or demonstrate how a brass instrument makes sound in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: The player's lips vibrate against a mouthpiece, setting air in the instrument vibrating.
misconceptions: An instrument belongs to the brass family only because its surface looks gold.
topics.question: What starts the sound in a trumpet?
topics.answer: The player's lips vibrate against a mouthpiece, setting air in the instrument vibrating.
topics.explanation: The vibration and air column produce the sound; the instrument's appearance alone does not explain it.
hints: What part of the player touches the mouthpiece?
What happens to create a vibration?
topics.activity: Use a labelled picture of a trumpet to mark the mouthpiece and trace a simple sound-production sequence; no instrument or mouthpiece sharing is needed.

topics.name: Microtones and pitch distinctions
topics.description: A microtone is an interval smaller than a semitone. Different musical traditions and individual performers can use pitch inflections or tuning approaches that do not fit every note neatly into a standard Western keyboard's semitone steps.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Elements of Music: Pitch, Phase 3 > Music, Year 8
objectives: Explain or demonstrate microtones and pitch distinctions in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: It is a smaller pitch interval than a semitone.
misconceptions: Every musical tradition uses only the same semitone steps as a standard Western keyboard.
topics.question: How does a microtone compare in size with a semitone?
topics.answer: It is a smaller pitch interval than a semitone.
topics.explanation: The term describes the size of the pitch difference, not how loudly the note is played.
hints: Does the question ask about pitch distance or volume?
Which interval is smaller than the semitone?
topics.activity: Draw a line from one pitch to another a semitone away and mark an imagined smaller interval between them; do not assume one tuning system applies to every tradition.

topics.name: Fermata and a held note
topics.description: A fermata is a notation symbol that asks a performer to hold a note or rest longer than its written duration. The length of the hold depends on the musical context and, in an ensemble, the shared direction of performers or conductor.
topics.locator: PDF p. 33, Elements of Music: Expressive elements, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate fermata and a held note in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Hold the note longer than its written value.
misconceptions: A fermata always means exactly two extra beats in every performance.
topics.question: What does a fermata above a note indicate?
topics.answer: Hold the note longer than its written value.
topics.explanation: The symbol alters the expected duration of that note rather than specifying an exact universal number of extra beats.
hints: Does the symbol relate to pitch or duration?
What happens to the note's duration?
topics.activity: Draw a four-beat sequence with one marked held note, then write how an ensemble might agree when to continue; use a notation reference for the symbol.
materials: paper and a fermata symbol reference

topics.name: A dotted rest
topics.description: A dot after a rest adds half the rest's original duration, just as it does for a dotted note. In 4/4 time, a dotted half rest occupies three beats of silence.
topics.locator: PDF p. 32, Elements of Music: Beat and rhythm, Phase 4 > Music, Year 10
objectives: Explain or demonstrate a dotted rest in the example.
evidence: Explains or demonstrates in the example: Three beats.
misconceptions: A rest has no duration because it is silent.
topics.question: How many beats of silence does a dotted half rest occupy in 4/4?
topics.answer: Three beats.
topics.explanation: A half rest lasts two beats and its dot adds one more beat, half of the original duration.
hints: How long is a half rest in 4/4?
How much duration does the dot add?
